commits.author: Claude
commits.message:
Merge GENESIS, and make its chain say which step has not run

PR #342 lands the full GENESIS 275 frontier surface: evolution engine,
scientist, ontology, metabolism, economic physics, venture organism, world
resilience, sensing/cognition, final frontier and the implementation ledger.
Merged whole -- nothing removed.

The closure-order memory conflicted; resolved by keeping both sides rather than
picking one. HEAD's 17:53 refresh is newer and stays, and three doctrine lines
only the branch carried are carried forward: that these two PRs are the software
finish line, that Claude Code is not for tiny tickets today, and that Claude
comments are not proof of Claude execution.

Two real defects, both found by running the surface rather than only testing it.

**The chain did not say what it was waiting for.** GENESIS runs gamechanger ->
evolve -> scientist -> ontology, each step reading what the last one wrote, and
each correctly refuses when its input is absent. On a host with no configured
provider that is the normal state, so an operator meets these refusals first --
and they reported a status and a path with no indication of which earlier step
had not run. Each now names the producing command, and a test asserts every
command named is one package.json actually defines, because a refusal that sends
you to a command that does not exist is worse than one that says nothing.

**The implementation ledger depended on what somebody had run locally.** Its
runtime-receipt scan was rooted at the repository unconditionally, so the same
commit produced a different ledger before and after `npm run genesis:evolve` --
and the test pinning idea 2 at SOURCE_AND_TEST_PRESENT broke the moment anyone
exercised the pipeline it was testing. The upgrade to
OBSERVED_INTERNAL_RUNTIME_RECEIPT was correct; the coupling was not.

Runtime receipts are now rooted separately from sources and tests, defaulting to
the repository so real runs are unchanged and a receipt still upgrades a status.
A caller needing the classification to depend only on the commit points it
somewhere clean. Verified both ways: the test passes with receipts present and
absent. GENESIS-LEDGER-01 kills the coupling if it returns.

Whole surface exercised end to end: all nine entry points exit 0 in chain order,
test:genesis 110/110.

commits.author: Claude
commits.message:
Merge Avengers, and make the arsenal chain say which step has not run

PR #364 activates the Avengers arsenal: local runtime discovery, callability
proof, evidence-routed squad planning and a canonically verified execution
guard. Merged whole -- nothing removed.

Exercised rather than only tested, and the chain has a reporting defect. It is
doctor -> plan -> tick, each step reading what the last one wrote, and all four
input paths threw into a generic handler that printed the raw error:

  AVENGERS_TICK_CRASHED / ENOENT: no such file or directory, open
  '.../artifacts/avengers-squad-plan.json'

That is the arsenal's most common state on this host, and it is not a crash.
Nothing is callable without a configured provider, so the planner correctly
refuses with no-callable-avenger for every node and writes no plan. The system
working as designed was being reported as a filesystem error about a filename.

A missing artifact now names the step that has not run, the command that
produces it, and -- this is the part that matters -- that the producing step may
itself legitimately refuse. Without that last clause an operator reads the
refusal as a second bug and goes looking for it. A malformed artifact is
distinguished from an absent one and says regenerate rather than repair by hand,
because a half-written artifact is worse than none: everything downstream would
treat whatever parsed as truth.

AVENGERS-INPUT-01 and -02 kill both halves. The second had to be re-anchored:
mutating `JSON.parse(text)` to `JSON.parse(text) || {}` changes no output for
any valid object, so it survived every test -- unfalsifiable rather than
untested. Anchored on the refusal branch, it kills.

commits.author: Claude
commits.message:
Regenerate canon alone, so it names a tree nothing has moved since

Canon on main named 9e46a541 while three source files had changed since -- the
browser resolver commit regenerated canon and moved source in the same commit,
so the artifact described a tree that was already one step behind by the time it
landed.

The freshness rule accepts canon naming an earlier commit only when nothing but
the canon artifacts has changed since, which is the whole point of it: canon
cannot name the commit that contains it, but it can be exact about everything
else. That only holds if a regeneration is its own commit. This one is: two
files, both canon.

commits.author: Claude
commits.message:
Fix the four tests main is shipping red

Compared failure sets rather than assuming: origin/main fails 24 tests, this
branch failed 7, and every one of the 7 was also red on main. Nothing here was
caused by the merge. Three were the canon figures; these are the other four.

**The autonomy followup could never pass.** The receipt ledger needs store.add
and store.get, and the test's fake store had neither, so the job refused with
store-atomic-add-and-get-required. The refusal is correct -- an execution receipt
is written under a deterministic id precisely so a duplicate tick cannot write a
second one, and a store that cannot refuse the duplicate cannot provide that.
The fake now models the real one: add throws on a repeated id, get returns what
is there. A fake that accepted every add would let a double-write pass here and
fail in production.

**The model admission fixture had no provider**, and the module requires one, so
that test also arrived red and stayed red. The requirement is the half worth
keeping: an admission that cannot name who served the model is exactly what the
routing law exists to refuse, since fallback must preserve provider identity in
receipts. Fixture repaired, and the gap it was hiding given its own test.

**The brain's capability count was pinned at 8 and the registry now holds 11.**
Updated rather than loosened -- registering a supplier should arrive as a failing
test rather than as three more capabilities nobody decided on, and this
assertion is what said so. The three new ids are named individually, so a
supplier cannot be swapped for another without saying so.

commits.author: Claude
commits.message:
Count a hundred replays where the uniqueness lives

The last suite stalling the real-database gate. It drove a hundred webhook
replays from the client and counted the ConflictErrors, and inside node:test
that wedges: after about a hundred rejected pg queries the next one never
returns. The suite stopped rather than failed and took the rest of the gate with
it, which is why ~180 real-database tests behind it had gone unrun.

The convenient answer would have been "the database is slow", and it was wrong.
Measured before concluding anything:

- the same loop with no conflicts does 200 queries in 61ms;
- with conflicts through a pool, it stops at ~55 iterations, and at that moment
  the server reports no backends for the database at all;
- with conflicts on one dedicated Client, it stops at the same ~100 errors;
- the identical loop outside node:test does 300 conflicts in 90ms.

So it is the test runner, not the driver, the pool, the count, or this code --
and production is not implicated, which is why nothing in src/ changed here.

The replay count stays at a hundred; the rejections stop crossing the process
boundary. Postgres runs its own hundred in a PL/pgSQL loop and reports how many
the index refused, which tests the constraint more directly than counting
exceptions in JavaScript did. The JSON store keeps the client loop, because its
uniqueness is in JavaScript and that is where it has to be exercised.

Falsified before being believed: removing UNIQUE from provider_event_id fails it
with "postgres: replay must be refused after the first, not absorbed".

commits.author: Claude
commits.message:
Test the recovery lock instead of hoping two workers overlap

The Gmail concurrency test started two recovery workers with Promise.all and
asserted that exactly one claimed the row. On a fast disposable database they
stopped overlapping, both claimed it, and the test failed.

Both claims were legitimate. RESULT_UNCERTAIN is itself an unresolved status, so
once the first worker commits the row back to RESULT_UNCERTAIN it is a valid
candidate again -- and nothing was double-dispatched, which is the invariant
that actually matters. "Exactly one worker claims it" was never true of
sequential runs. A concurrency test that depends on losing a race proves nothing
on the days it wins one, and the file's own comment had already talked itself
into believing the both-claimed branch was "excluded by PostgreSQL semantics".

So the overlap is made real rather than hoped for: the first worker's
transaction is held open, and the second must find nothing to claim while it is.
That is FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED being tested rather than assumed, and
RECOVERY-LOCK-01 now kills its removal.

Three smaller things fell out of proving it can fail:

- The dispatch-count assertion folded in the adapter that performed the original
  authorized dispatch, whose count is 1 by design, so it would have passed or
  failed for the wrong reason. Counted on the recovery worker now, with the
  original dispatch asserted separately as exactly one.
- The holder is released in a finally. It was released after the assertion, so a
  failure left the holder's transaction parked and pool.end() waiting on it --
  the suite stalled instead of reporting the failure it had just found.
- lock_timeout and statement_timeout are set per connection rather than through
  the `options` connection parameter, which was tried first and silently did
  nothing. A timeout that is not in force looks like protection and is worse
  than none.

Verified in both directions: unmodified 4/4; with SKIP LOCKED removed, the named
test fails rather than the file stalling.

commits.author: Claude
commits.message:
Run the transition-guard check inside the server instead of across the wire

The exhaustive (from,to) check walked 132 pairs from the client -- BEGIN, an
insert, a few updates, ROLLBACK -- roughly six hundred round trips. On this
container that is not merely slow. Around the 122nd transaction the connection
stops responding: the backend sits `active`, waits on nothing, holds no lock and
ignores statement_timeout, because it is blocked writing a result to a socket.
Nothing times it out from either side, so the suite stopped rather than failed.

Three isolation fixes were tried and none of them moved it -- a pool, then one
dedicated client, then a fresh connection per pair, each stopping in the same
place. That is what identified the cost as the round trips themselves rather
than anything held in a session or a pool, and it is why the earlier diagnosis
("the pool was empty after roughly 120 of the 132 pairs") was wrong about the
mechanism while being right about where it stopped.

The loop now runs in PL/pgSQL: four statements instead of six hundred. Each
attempt gets its own subtransaction so a rejection rolls that pair back, and an
accepted row is deleted afterwards because the partial unique index on
business_key is part of what is under test. Only the attempt is guarded -- a
failure while walking the legal setup path is a broken fixture, not a verdict,
so it fails loudly rather than being recorded as a rejection the database never
made.

The check is stronger than before, not weaker: the client no longer takes any
part in deciding what the database accepted. Falsified before being believed --
claiming every transition is legal fails with Postgres's own message, "illegal
execution transition: <new> -> DISPATCHING".

Also removes an unref that was masking this. It stopped a stuck socket pinning
the event loop, but with nothing else pending the loop drained mid-query and the
runner cancelled the test with "Promise resolution is still pending but the
event loop has already resolved" -- deterministically, every run. A socket must
be a reason to stay alive while the test runs and stop being one when it ends:
that is a destroy in the finally, not an unref at the top.

Gate: 23 suites, 177 tests, 175 pass. Two suites still fail and are being worked
next; before this, three did and the file above was the one stopping the run.

Three guards -- HYG-01, HYG-02, MONEY-17 -- hung inside a full run and killed

fresh database each, and stuck backends from earlier suites terminated before

complete isolation is cheaper than continuing to guess.

commits.author: Claude
commits.message:
Break the hang cascade, and take one bounded second look at a hang

Three guards -- HYG-01, HYG-02, MONEY-17 -- kept reporting SUITE_TIMED_OUT in a
full run and KILLED alone. The failing set drifted later each run, which is the
signature of a cascade rather than three unreliable tests.

A suite killed at its deadline can leave a PostgreSQL backend that never notices
its client is gone: the stall the postgres-real runner already documents. Each
one holds a connection and keeps working, so the first hang in a run makes the
next one likelier. Those clients are provably gone -- the runner killed the
process that opened them -- so they are terminated before each database-backed
mutation, reclaiming the connection rather than interrupting live work.

With the cascade cut, a hang can still happen, and a guard that was never tested
is the one thing this file must not leave standing. So a SUITE_TIMED_OUT gets
one second attempt, against the reclaimed state rather than as a repeat of an
unchanged mechanism.

This is deliberately not "retry until it passes":
- only a hang qualifies, because that is the verdict meaning no measurement was
  taken. A SURVIVED or a KILLED is a measurement and stands on the first run.
- exactly one attempt, no loop.
- whatever it finds is recorded, including another hang.
- the row is printed as "(second attempt after a hang)", so it can never be read
  as a clean first pass.

A test asserts that shape rather than leaving it to review, because a retry loop
is how a mutation gate quietly stops meaning anything.

commits.author: Claude
commits.message:
Stop a hang beside a kill from erasing the kill

The rule added in the last commit -- node's own test deadline classifies as
SUITE_TIMED_OUT -- was too broad, and the diagnostics caught it immediately.

MONEY-05 and HYG-03 each reported the exact assertion the mutation was written
to break ("READY content is not terminal and must survive", "manual paid flag
plus positive revenue row is never treated as cleared payment proof") in a file
where a different test stalled. Both were recorded as untested. A genuine kill
was being discarded because of unrelated noise beside it.

An assertion that failed is the evidence this whole file exists to collect: a
named invariant broke when the guard was removed. Another test hanging does not
undo that. So an ERR_ASSERTION failure now wins over a co-occurring hang.

The concession runs one way only, and TIMEOUT-03 exists to keep it that way: a
hang with no assertion behind it is still never a kill, which is the property
that stops a loaded machine from manufacturing evidence. Our own wall-clock kill
still dominates everything, because it cuts the output at an arbitrary point and
nothing in it can be trusted.

HYG-01, HYG-02, HYG-03 and MONEY-05 all KILLED on re-run.

commits.author: Claude
commits.message:
Stop the war from creating the load that made three guards untestable

Three database-backed guards kept reporting SUITE_DID_NOT_RUN in a full run and
KILLED when run alone. The new diagnostics said why on the first try, which is
the point of them: the suites were not failing, they were hanging -- cut off at
node's 120s deadline, in suites that finish in under a second on their own.

The load was self-inflicted. The sandbox copied 116MB of node_modules for each
of 160 mutations, roughly 18GB of I/O per run, and under that the same
PostgreSQL stall the postgres-real runner was repaired for became reachable: a
backend asleep writing to a socket nobody is reading. The gate was reporting
"not tested" about guards it had itself made untestable.

node_modules is now symlinked. Nothing mutates a dependency, so the tree can be
shared -- and applyMutation now refuses any anchor inside node_modules, because
sharing means a mutation pointed there would edit the real dependency tree of
the repository it is supposed to be testing a copy of. No registered mutation
does; SANDBOX-01 is there so none ever can.

Two smaller repairs came out of the same investigation:

- Node's per-test deadline now classifies as SUITE_TIMED_OUT. It arrives as an
  ordinary non-zero exit whose TAP summary may never have been written, so it
  read as SUITE_DID_NOT_RUN -- true, but it sends a reader looking for a broken
  import instead of a stall. TIMEOUT-02 kills it.
- Non-verdicts now carry the suite lines that look like a cause. A gate that
  says SUITE_DID_NOT_RUN and nothing else is a dead end, and the run that knows
  the answer is the one being discarded.

commits.author: Claude
commits.message:
Give each database-backed mutation its own database

The full war reported five guards as SUITE_DID_NOT_RUN -- HYG-01, HYG-02,
HYG-03, BILL-03 and MONEY-17. Every one of them KILLS when run alone. All 160
mutations shared a single database, so a suite that left rows behind broke the
setup of every Postgres suite scheduled after it, and the gate was measuring the
order it happened to visit them in rather than the guards themselves.

SUITE_DID_NOT_RUN is at least honest about that -- it is the verdict that exists
precisely so a suite which never ran cannot be read as a mutant that died or a
guard that held. But five guards permanently in that state is a gate reporting
"not killed" about protections that are, in fact, held up.

Same repair as the postgres-real runner, which had the same defect: a fresh
database per unit of work. Not dropped afterwards, for the same reason recorded
there -- these live in a disposable embedded server, and reclaiming them is how
that runner acquired an unbounded wait on a backend that cannot be stopped.

Verified: all five KILLED with a database each.

commits.author: Claude
commits.message:
Bound the mutation war's suites, and stop journaling skips

Two defects, both found by the war stalling in front of me.

**No suite deadline.** The war ran each killing suite with no timeout, so one
suite that never returned left the whole run in ep_poll with no output, no
verdict, and nothing to say which mutation it was on -- thirteen minutes of a
run went that way before anyone read /proc. A real database makes that hang
reachable, which the postgres-real runner already found the hard way; the war
never got the same repair.

Each test is now bounded at 120s so most hangs surface as an ordinary failure,
with a 600s wall deadline as the backstop for a suite wedged before the runner
starts counting. A killed suite gets its own verdict: SUITE_TIMED_OUT, which
lands in "not tested at all" and fails the run rather than being absorbed into
KILLED or SURVIVED. It dominates the exit code deliberately -- a suite killed
mid-run can emit a partial TAP stream carrying a failure count, which would
otherwise read as a mutant that died when nothing finished.

**Skips were journaled.** SKIPPED_NEEDS_POSTGRES says this host had no database.
That is a fact about the machine, not a judgement about the guard, and replaying
it into a later run on a machine that has one would report a capability gap that
no longer exists and quietly stop testing that guard for good -- the same shape
as the CRAWL-01 problem the browser resolver was written to end, arriving
through the mechanism built to fix it.

The rule lives in appendVerdict rather than at the call site, because it is the
journal's invariant and a caller that forgets it should not be able to write
one. Everything else survives, including the bad news: SURVIVED, SUITE_TIMED_OUT
and ANCHOR_AMBIGUOUS are all remembered, or the record could only ever improve.

TIMEOUT-01 and JOURNAL-03 kill both. JOURNAL-03's anchor had to move into
mutation-journal.mjs for the same self-reference reason as the browser resolver:
an anchor quoted in the registry that lives in the registry's own file matches
twice.

commits.author: Claude
commits.message:
Make the mutation war survive being interrupted

The full war takes over an hour against a real database, and this host restarts
its container under load. Four consecutive runs were killed in flight, each one
discarding every verdict it had already earned, so the summary line the
readiness artifact quotes had never once been produced for the current registry.
Restarting it hopefully a fifth time is not a plan.

MUTATION_WAR_JOURNAL appends each verdict the moment it is decided and replays
it on the next run, so an interrupted war resumes instead of starting over.
Replayed rows are labelled in the output; a run that says KILLED should be able
to say whether it watched that happen.

A resumable gate is also a gate that can report work nobody did, so the binding
is the feature rather than a detail. Every entry carries a hash of the mutation
that earned it -- file, anchor, replacement and killing suites. Move any of
them and the entry stops matching and the mutation runs again, because a verdict
is about a specific guard in a specific place, not about an id. Suite order is
deliberately not part of it: a cosmetic reordering should not discard an hour of
real evidence, or the resume is one nobody uses.

Five tests hold this down, because its failure mode is a green summary line
rather than a red one, and a green lie is not something a later run corrects:
an id alone cannot claim a verdict, a wrong or absent fingerprint is refused, a
damaged journal loses entries rather than inventing them, a missing journal is
empty rather than an error, and a later verdict supersedes an earlier one in
both directions -- a SURVIVED recorded after a KILLED must stick, or the record
can only ever improve. JOURNAL-01 and JOURNAL-02 confirm both halves are killed
when weakened.

commits.author: Claude
commits.message:
Classify the twelve modules PR #329 landed with no entry point

The reachability ratchet went red on the merge: Frontier Operator (eight
modules) and Open Model Universe (four) arrived implemented, tested, green and
unreachable. That is the exact condition the ratchet exists to catch, and it
caught it -- #329 was red on this check before the merge, not because of it.

Classified rather than wired. Wiring an orchestrator that nothing schedules
would create an orchestrator with nothing to orchestrate, and an orchestrator
that runs is precisely the thing not to switch on before its consequence path is
decided. Two gates registered, each naming what would release it: a host that
drives a Goal Contract through the operator under existing authority and budget
gates, and a configured open-model runtime endpoint with model identity and
pricing evidence.

open-model-runtime-executor is not among them. It is already reachable through
the model factory, which is why production reachability rose 139 -> 140 rather
than staying flat: the executor is wired and reports runtime-absent,
model-identity-absent, runtime-endpoint-absent, pricing-evidence-absent and
explicitly-disabled, so the new provider is live in the graph and unable to
execute anything. That is the correct shape.

Two provider-list tests also broke on the fifth provider, and they broke
differently:

- agent-mesh-entry-point pinned the exact list. Updated, not loosened -- adding
  a provider should arrive as a failing test rather than as an unnoticed fifth
  executor. Strengthened with an assertion that a provider which is not ready
  says what is missing.
- agent-mesh-activation-evidence read the sandbox by array position. It found
  the wrong row when a provider was inserted ahead of it, reporting a defect in
  the sandbox gate that did not exist -- and it would equally have hidden one
  that did. Now found by name.

Verified independently of both: every one of the five providers is not ready by
default, and open-model carries five blockers.

commits.author: Claude
commits.message:
Converge with PR #329 and make the browser gate look before it skips

Two lanes harvested the same night-convergence branch and diverged. Neither head
carried the other's work: #329 had Frontier Operator, the Open Model Universe,
the mutation-registry anchor-integrity test and the owner's PayPal.me binding;
this branch had the proposal-eligibility fix, the canon-freshness partition, the
repaired real-database runner and six more mutations. Merged rather than picked,
with two conflicts resolved deliberately.

first-cash-canary-packet: this branch's implementation is the base (597 lines
against 118, bound to the payment-rail doctor, the canary guard and the
canonical fulfilment machine), with #329's payment-link semantics absorbed into
it. That absorption fixed a conflation of my own: WHAT_PAYMENT_LINK answered
"none yet" out of the rail doctor's state, so a packet reported no payment link
while the owner had supplied a public one. A destination and a rail are
different facts. The link is PREPARED; reconciliation is still
EXTERNAL_PROOF_REQUIRED; paymentRailLiveReady stays false and canContact with
it. PAYMENT_LINK_IS_NOT_CLEARED_PAYMENT_PROOF rides on every packet, present or
absent, because the moment that field goes missing is the moment paymentLink
reads as revenue. Non-HTTPS and unparseable links fail closed to null.

mutation-war: union of both registries, verified by set comparison rather than
by reading the diff -- 154 entries, no duplicate ids, nothing in #329's 148 that
the merge dropped.

And the browser gate now looks for a browser. It read CHROMIUM_PATH and nothing
else, and nothing in this repository sets it, so on a machine with Chromium
installed the war reported SKIPPED_NEEDS_BROWSER for a guard it could have
exercised -- while still printing "0 not killed". In a summary line a skip that
cannot be helped and a skip that could are indistinguishable.

Detection is the kind of convenience that becomes a fabrication if it guesses,
so it only accepts paths that exist and are executable, respects a declared
install root instead of also scanning /opt behind it, and returns '' rather than
a plausible-looking path when it finds nothing -- an honest skip survives.
A declared CHROMIUM_PATH stays authoritative and is still checked, because a
variable pointing at nothing is a misconfiguration, not a browser.

It lives in scripts/resolve-chromium.mjs rather than inside the registry: the
registry stores anchors as literal source strings, so a mutation of a function
in that same file matches its own registration and resolves ANCHOR_AMBIGUOUS.
BROWSER-01 and BROWSER-02 kill it; CRAWL-01 now runs by default rather than
skipping, and kills.

commits.message:
Make the doctor and the freshness test agree on what canon describes

The canon-drift row went red again the moment a handoff document was committed.
The doctor's probe asked whether *anything* had changed since the commit canon
names, so a file canon makes no claim about -- a handoff, a receipt, a README --
counted as drift. That is the always-red failure this row was just repaired for,
arriving from the other side: the previous version could never be satisfied by
regenerating canon, this one could never be satisfied by writing prose.

Both checks now partition the tree the same way, and a test asserts they always
will. Two answers to one question is how a row goes quiet -- the suite stays
green while the doctor reports a gap nobody can close, or the reverse.

This is the second loosening of this row, and the gap it opens is every file
outside src/, scripts/, config/ and migrations/, so it carries the proof:

- describesSource is exported and exercised directly: real source counts, the
  three canon artifacts do not, prose does not, and the exemption does not
  extend from config/system-readiness-input.json to a .bak of it or to the
  reachability classification beside it.
- sourceUnchangedSince is exercised against real git, because a probe hardcoded
  to `true` would pass every other test here and report canon fresh forever. It
  refuses a malformed SHA, an empty one, and a well-formed SHA naming no commit,
  rather than reading an unanswerable comparison as freshness.
- CANON-03 and CANON-04 confirm both are killed when weakened.

Also carries docs/handoffs/CLAUDE_OMEGA_CLOSURE_2026-09-03.md, which landed in
the canon commit, and the updated docs/CURRENT_HANDOFF.json.

commits.author: Claude
commits.message:
Stop counting the generator's own input as source the canon describes

The canon-staleness check treated everything under config/ as source, which
included config/system-readiness-input.json -- the file `npm run readiness`
reads. Regenerating canon rewrites that file in the same commit as the two
artifacts it produces, so every correct regeneration reported itself stale.
No generator can emit a tree in which its own input has not just moved.

That is the always-red failure the check's own comment warns about, arriving
by the back door: "a check that is always red is a check people turn off."

The exclusion is three named paths, not a config/ prefix, because a prefix
would also exempt the reachability classification and the policy files beside
it. It is safe in the direction that matters: the readiness input records what
was measured rather than how the system behaves, so it cannot make canon
describe a system that no longer exists, and a wrong figure in it is caught by
the figures test, which reads the tree rather than trusting either artifact.

A loosening of this check fails silently by never firing again, so it carries
the same duty of proof as the last one. Three tests in the discrimination suite
exercise the predicate the shipped file actually defines -- src/, scripts/,
migrations/ and the rest of config/ still make canon stale; the exemption does
not extend to a .bak of the exempt file -- and CANON-02 confirms widening it
into a directory exemption is killed.

commits.author: Claude
commits.message:
Make canon freshness a question canon can actually answer

The canon-drift row demanded that docs/CURRENT_SYSTEM_STATE.md name the current
head. It cannot: regenerating canon produces a commit, and that commit changes
the head the artifact would have had to name. The row was therefore permanently
open no matter how fresh canon was -- and a row that is always red is a row its
reader learns to skip, so the day canon really does drift it looks identical.

The honest question is not whether canon names HEAD but whether canon still
describes this source. Canon naming an earlier commit is fresh when nothing
except the canon artifacts has changed since: the source it describes is then
byte-for-byte the source that is here. Anything else moving is drift, which is
the whole point of the row.

The probe refuses on any error rather than assuming freshness -- an unreadable
history is not evidence that the source stood still -- and a caller that
supplies no probe at all gets the refusing default, not a free pass.

Verified both ways against the real tree: with only canon changed since the
named commit the gap closes, and appending one line to src/effect-ledgers.mjs
brings it straight back. The test pins five cases including the two ways a
caller could get freshness for nothing.

softwareGaps is now empty. That is the founder-absence doctor's own derived
answer, from probes against the tree rather than anything asserted, and it is
the mission's exit condition for removable software work.

commits.author: Claude
commits.message:
Stop reclaiming per-suite databases; a disposable server needs no housekeeping

Two attempts to drop each database after its suite ended the same way. A suite
that overran its timeout leaves a PostgreSQL backend nothing can stop: it sits
active writing results to a socket whose client is gone, so it never reaches a
point where a cancel is honoured. DROP DATABASE waits on it. WITH (FORCE) waits
on it too, because FORCE still has to terminate that backend. And
statement_timeout does not govern that wait -- a ten-second budget was observed
still sitting there after three minutes thirty-eight.

Each attempt put the hang back one layer above the layer the per-test timeout
had just fixed, which is the same mistake twice with a different SQL verb.

The databases live inside an embedded PostgreSQL torn down when the run ends, so
there was never anything to reclaim. Creating them is what buys the isolation;
deleting them buys nothing and was costing the entire gate.

commits.author: Claude
commits.message:
Force-drop the per-suite database so one stalled suite cannot stop the run

The per-database change moved the hang rather than removing it. A suite whose
statement never returns gets timed out by node:test, but node:test cannot close
the PostgreSQL connection that test opened, and the statement on it keeps
running -- observed directly: a `DROP DATABASE IF EXISTS
"ubpg_18_tests_payment_recovery_war_test_mjs"` sitting active while an
`INSERT INTO revenue_events` from the abandoned suite was still live on the
database being dropped, with two more backends queued behind it on an object
lock.

So the runner hung one layer above the layer the per-test timeout had just
fixed, and for the same underlying reason: something waits for a client that is
never coming back.

DROP DATABASE ... WITH (FORCE) terminates the backends first, with a fallback to
the plain form for servers older than PostgreSQL 13. An overrunning suite now
costs its own two minutes and nothing else's, which is what a bounded gate has
to mean.

commits.author: Claude
commits.message:
Give each real-database suite its own database

Serial execution was not enough. These suites recover *stuck* rows, and they
find them by sweeping the shared tables with deliberately broad limits (1000,
500, 50) -- which is correct, because a production recovery worker does not know
which rows are its own. Pointed at one shared database, a later suite's worker
claims rows an earlier suite left behind.

That is what "two concurrent recovery workers converge on exactly one outcome"
was failing on: neither worker claimed its row. The readiness note already
recorded that failure once and attributed it to file-level parallelism. It
reproduces at --test-concurrency=1, so parallelism was not the cause; sharing
the database was. Run alone, the suite passes 4/4.

Each file now gets a freshly created database on the same server, dropped
immediately after. Suites can sweep as broadly as production does and see only
their own rows, and a failure means what it says.

commits.author: Claude
commits.message:
Bound every test in the real-database gate

The stall was chased to its actual mechanism and it is not UberBond's SQL.

The PostgreSQL backend sleeps in `sock_alloc_send_pskb` — blocked writing
results to a client socket nobody is draining — burning zero CPU, holding no
lock, blocked by no other session. Every Node process in the tree sits idle in
`ep_poll` at the same moment. Neither side times the other out, so the run stops
and stays stopped. Ruled out along the way: lock contention (pg_blocking_pids
empty), a runaway trigger (zero utime and stime over a six-second sample), and
fsync on throttled container storage (still stalls with fsync, synchronous_commit
and full_page_writes all off — kept anyway, since a database deleted at the end
of the run has no durability to buy).

It is not a production defect. Each hanging statement was replayed on a fresh
connection and completed correctly in under a tenth of a second; it takes the
accumulated session state of a long suite to reproduce. Classified as
infrastructure, which is the distinction the engineering law asks for, and
recorded rather than hidden.

So the gate is made bounded instead. `--test-timeout=120000` applies to every
suite it runs, two minutes being far more than any of them needs and short
enough that a stall surfaces the same day. Combined with the per-test timeout
and the socket unref in the state-machine suite, the gate now always terminates
and always reports.

That is the whole point. This gate had never finished, so the roughly 180
real-database tests behind the first stall had never run — and nothing ever said
so, because a suite that hangs produces no output to disbelieve. It now runs
past it.

commits.author: Claude
commits.message:
Make the real-database gate finish, and say so when it cannot

`npm run test:postgres-real` has never completed. It runs
tests/omnia-v9-external-effect-state-machine.test.mjs, stops inside it, and
waits — with every assertion up to that point passing and nothing printed. The
roughly 180 real-database tests scheduled after that file had therefore never
executed once, and no run ever reported a problem, because a suite that hangs
reports nothing at all. A stale runner from a previous session was found still
sitting in the same place after ten hours.

Localized exactly. The walk stalls on the pair ABORTED_BEFORE_DISPATCH ->
PREPARED, at the UPDATE that moves the row PREPARED -> ABORTED_BEFORE_DISPATCH:
the transition that releases the business key from the partial unique index.
The backend sits `active` with no wait event, is blocked by no other session,
and ignores `statement_timeout` set both as client config and as an explicit
session SET.

It is not a production defect, and that was checked rather than assumed: the
same insert-then-transition sequence on a fresh connection is applied and then
correctly refused in under a tenth of a second. It requires the accumulated
session state of the ~122 preceding rolled-back transactions. The migration,
both triggers and the transition guard are sound.

Three defects in the test harness are fixed:

- `await client.query('ROLLBACK').catch(() => {})` does not catch the
  synchronous throw a dead client raises. The throw escaped the finally block
  and skipped `release()`, permanently removing a connection from the pool.
- The pool bought nothing — the pairs are checked serially — and could be
  exhausted by the above, after which `pool.connect()` waited for a client that
  was never coming. It is now one dedicated connection.
- `statement_timeout` passed as client config is silently ignored by some driver
  versions. A timeout not actually in force is worse than none, because it looks
  like protection. It is now set on the session.

None of those was the cause, and the remaining stall is recorded as a real
finding rather than papered over. What changed is that the gate now ends: a
120-second test timeout turns the silence into a failure, and unref'ing the
socket stops the abandoned query pinning the event loop and hanging the runner
one layer up. The suite reports `not ok`, exits, and every test after it runs.

commits.author: Claude
commits.message:
A proposal cannot mark its own win as commercial truth

`summarizeProposalOutcome` returned `commercialTruthEligible: true` from three
values the caller typed: a status of WON, a positive `revenueCleared`, and a
currency string. Nothing pointed outside the process. The existing test asserted
exactly that shape and passed, so the defect was covered rather than caught.

The field name is what makes it dangerous. Elsewhere in this repository
`validateCanonicalSprintPaymentTruth` recomputes a digest, requires a live
one-time provider event, rejects a reference marked sandbox or synthetic, and
demands three-witness claim boundaries before anything is called cleared. A
neighbouring function answering "yes, eligible for commercial truth" off
self-report invites a future caller to use the cheap one. The module is
currently unreachable, which is the best possible moment to fix it: a latent
defect behind a gate becomes a real one the day the gate opens.

Eligibility now also requires a payment reference that could have come from
outside — EXTERNAL origin, EXTERNAL_PAYMENT class, a `payment:` reference, and
not one marked sandbox, synthetic, fixture, fake or test. It deliberately does
not verify the payment; that remains the canonical validator's job. It
establishes only that the caller is pointing at something other than itself,
which is the minimum before the word "cleared" is allowed in the answer. The
returned boundary says so in full: eligible for canonical payment validation,
not cleared revenue.

The test now walks four near-misses — internal origin, wrong evidence class, a
CRM reference rather than a payment one, and a sandbox payment — before the one
that passes. Two mutations hold both halves and both are killed.

commits.author: Claude
commits.message:
Anchor the quarantine guard where it actually decides

Registering a mutation on the reconciliation lookup's quarantine filter showed
it SURVIVED, and the reason is worth recording: the wrapper filters
authenticated/quarantineReason/eligibleForReconciliation, then hands the result
straight to deriveCurrentPostalState, which filters the same three fields again.
Removing the wrapper's copy changes no output for any input. It survived not
because nothing tests it but because nothing can — a redundant guard is
unfalsifiable, and an unfalsifiable guard in a mutation registry is a green
result that means nothing.

The mutation now anchors in the evidence module's filter, which is the one that
decides, and it is killed. The wrapper's copy stays as defence in depth with a
note saying which of the two is load-bearing.

The test that goes with it feeds five separately inadmissible rows — unsigned,
malformed, unknown event type, unauthenticated-but-unquarantined, and eligible
flag off — each otherwise complete and each claiming
`provenance: 'AUTHENTICATED_POSTAL_WEBHOOK'` and
`eligibleForReconciliation: true`, which is what a forged delivery looks like
once it has been recorded. None may reach reconciliation, none may manufacture
a contradiction, and the admissible row still comes through.

Second-sweep audit of the sender-evidence consumer, the only thing in the Postal
path that mutates state from a webhook: it requires authentication, refuses any
quarantined or reconciliation-eligible event, matches sender domains by exact
equality rather than suffix, derives a deterministic event id from the
occurrence key so a redelivery cannot double-write, and only ever pauses. No
finding.

commits.author: Claude
commits.message:
Hold the merged rules down: ten mutations and a hostile sweep

The merge decided several rules by choosing between two implementations. A rule
that was chosen but not defended is a rule the next merge can quietly choose
differently, so each one now has something that fails when it goes.

Ten mutations, covering what this merge actually settled:

- CONV-01 caller-asserted provider state cannot open a LIVE route
- CONV-02 the gateway reads AI_GATEWAY_*, never a prefix derived from its id
- CONV-03/04 negative rates and unparseable verification dates are not pricing
- CONV-05 a record this system generated cannot verify itself
- CONV-06 the fifth qualified conversation with no paid pilot ends the canary
- CONV-07 the first-cash offer stays bound to the canonical Lead-Path SKU
- CONV-08 CODE_READY needs observed operation, not an absence of complaints
- POSTAL-409 a 409 is ambiguous, never a definite rejection
- POSTAL-ZERO no webhook row is not proof that nothing was submitted

138 registered mutations become 148, and every anchor resolves to exactly one
site.

The hostile suite attacks nine ways a caller could get a stronger answer than
the evidence supports. Two of them found nothing because the protection already
held, so both were verified by removing the protection and watching the test
fail: dropping the unowned-assignment refusal lets `send.attacker.example` be
planned under an owned root, and restoring the convergence stub's
`if (gaps.length) overall = 'DISTRIBUTION_BLOCKED'` lets an unfinished module
hide a missing credential. A green sweep that survives deleting the guard is not
evidence.

Also closed here, all four verified failing on a clean worktree of acc7d132
first:

- The customer-binding fixture now carries the cleared-payment stage reference,
  the canonical product and the three-witness boundary its validator demands.
  The validator was right; the fixture was three requirements behind it.
- DomainDNSError is no longer asserted to prove a message was submitted. It is
  an event about the sending domain's records, it can arrive when nothing was
  ever sent, and reading it as acceptance would let a domain-wide
  misconfiguration certify a send that never happened. It reconciles to
  UNCERTAIN, and the adapter's own status set already agreed.
- Three modules main merged with no entry point are resolved: the canary guard
  by wiring it, and the Genome admission step and proposal engine by classifying
  them against gates that state what would release them.
- Three mutation anchors that pointed into the replaced files now point at the
  equivalent guards in the versions that survived.

Security audit of the changed surface: no shell-interpolating subprocess call,
no fetch on a caller-supplied URL, 0 dependency vulnerabilities. The Postal
route refuses before reading when unconfigured, caps the body at 1 MiB before
parsing, verifies over exact bytes, declines to reinterpret Postal's legacy
SHA-1 header as SHA-256, and answers a storage failure without echoing the
connection string. Sender evidence can only be applied by an authenticated DNS
event and only pauses, never enables.

commits.author: Claude
commits.message:
Merge main and the night convergence harvest, resolved by verified semantics

Both lanes built the same six capabilities under different names. The merge
picked per file by what each version actually protects, not by which branch was
newer or larger.

Main's work wins where it is genuinely stronger:

- The Postal evidence layer handles DomainDNSError sender evidence, rejects
  future-dated events and orders lifecycle states monotonically, none of which
  the Ragnarok version did. Its reconciliation lookup filters quarantined rows
  at the wrapper, which is a real boundary.
- The Postal adapter is v1.3.0 and already carries the dispatch timeout, the
  executionId-optional reconcile and the provenance check the Ragnarok branch
  was built to add. Only the shared-primitives refactor was unique, and it stays
  where the Gmail adapter uses it.
- lead-path-sprint-fulfillment composes the canonical service-fulfillment engine
  and binds the sprint to a SKU, a recomputed payment-truth digest and a
  provider event that may not read as sandbox or synthetic. The Ragnarok branch
  had reimplemented a parallel state machine beside it; that duplicate and its
  test are gone.
- The executor factory's single `ai-gateway` identity matches the provider list
  main's own entry-point test asserts. The Ragnarok alias would have broken it.

The convergence harvest wins on one rule and loses on four files:

- LIVE routing may no longer be opened by caller-supplied provider states. Four
  booleans anybody can type are not an activation, and the test that used to
  prove LIVE worked that way now proves it refuses, with a receipt-derived route
  beside it so the legitimate door is still shown to open. Supplying both
  receipts and states reports the ambiguity as well, which that rewrite had
  swallowed.
- Its four "harvested" doctors were 33-, 61-, 64- and 83-line stubs that take
  the answer as an argument: `softwareGaps: []` in, `CODE_READY` out. The
  measuring implementations are kept and now export the convergence names, so
  either vocabulary reaches one answer. In the classifier a software gap can no
  longer mask a credential blocker, and absent elapsed-observation proof the
  verdict is never CODE_READY.
- The rewrite had also stripped the comments explaining why observed quotas only
  tighten, why an unknown audience is refused on a capped provider and why two

commits.author: Claude
commits.message:
Merge current main and reconcile one gateway wearing two identities

Main advanced nine commits while this branch was working, and it brought its
own AI Gateway executor. Three files collided.

The router and the activation-receipt validator turned out byte-identical to
main -- that work had already landed -- so there was nothing to reconcile. The
gateway executor was a real conflict: main's 121-line implementation against
this branch's 639-line one. Main's is newer and on main, so main's wins. The
longer file was not better evidence, it was just longer.

Main's version carries the same defect the discarded one had, and its test only
checked the success path, where no error message exists. A client that echoes
the request it failed on puts the Authorization header into its error text, and
three sites copied that text verbatim into a durable receipt. Scrubbed now, with
a test that drives the three failure paths that actually carry a message, and
GATEWAY-01 repointed at main's implementation where it kills.

The merge also produced a defect neither side had alone: two provider ids for
one gateway. `ai-gateway` arrived in main's API_PROVIDERS while this branch
added `vercel-ai-gateway` as a separate lane, so describeProviderReadiness
returned two rows for one credential. Worse, main's row derives its env prefix
by upper-casing the provider id, which yields AI-GATEWAY_API_KEY -- a variable
nobody sets. Measured with a fully configured gateway: `ai-gateway` reported
credential-absent while `vercel-ai-gateway` reported ready, from the same key.

Both halves matter. Readiness and execution disagreeing makes a working lane
look unavailable. Two rows for one credential is worse: executeWithFailover
reads a list of destinations, so an exhausted gateway appeared to be a chain
with somewhere left to go, and routing around it would have retried the same
provider under another name -- the one thing the routing law forbids while
looking exactly like the thing it permits. One canonical id now, an explicit
env-prefix map, the duplicate branch removed, and both spellings still build.

Seventeen tests for the Postal webhook path, which was production-reachable
through a route and had none. They sign with a real key pair rather than
stubbing verification, because a stubbed check proves the path runs and not
that the check works: a forged signature, a body signed for different bytes,
and an absent key are each refused; the recipient token and raw body never
survive normalization; a replay collapses to one row while two genuine message
ids stay two; a quarantined row is never offered to reconciliation; and a
storage failure cannot echo the connection string it failed on.

commits.author: Claude
commits.message:
Close the last software gaps the absence doctor could still measure

Four modules landed without tests and one canonical guard list did not know
about any of them. Both halves matter: an untested doctor is an opinion, and a
guard nobody mutates is decoration.

Six suites, forty-five tests. Written by driving each module rather than by
describing it, which is how the tests found the contracts the modules actually
have -- applySprintEvent returns an envelope carrying the new sprint,
evaluateDomainRecord takes the observation separately from the record and keys
provenance by kind, and a verification receipt needs provider origin, a real
event id, durability and a date within seven days.

Fourteen mutations registered into the canonical war, taking it from 124 to 138.
Thirteen died on the first run. CASH-01 survived: removing the requirement that
an accepted delivery carry customer-origin evidence broke nothing, because
every sprint the suite builds reaches acceptance through a machine that already
refuses the alternative. The clause is not defending the machine, it is
defending the count against a row the machine did not write -- a drifted
record, an older writer, a hand edit. Tested at that level now, it dies.

What the new guards hold: a stale activation receipt derives no live flags; a
receipt cannot loosen the registry's cold rule; an observed quota cannot raise
a researched one; a recipient cap is compared to a real audience; only an
authenticated Postal webhook row can reconcile; a bounce is acceptance with
negative delivery rather than provider rejection; contact needs every gate
rather than any gate; a record this system generated cannot verify itself; a
stale DNS reading stops verifying; and provider error text is scrubbed before
it can carry a credential into a receipt.

The founder-absence doctor now measures exactly one remaining software gap:
canon drift, which is the one that must be closed last.

commits.author: Claude
commits.message:
Test the sprint machine and the payment rail against their real contracts

Both modules arrived without tests, which for a fulfilment state machine and a
payment readiness doctor is the same as arriving without a claim: nothing
established that internal QA cannot accept a delivery on the customer's behalf,
or that five environment variables cannot amount to being able to take money.

The sprint suite drives the machine rather than describing it. Writing it found
that applySprintEvent returns a result envelope carrying the new sprint under
.sprint, so feeding the envelope back reports valid-sprint-state-required --
which reads like a rejected transition and is a caller mistake. Worth a comment
in the test, because the next caller will do the same thing.

What the tests hold up: a commercial sprint cannot open on an internally
asserted payment; a delivery cannot be accepted by its seller even when the
event carries the customer's evidence class; silence is a distinct outcome from
acceptance and counts as zero deliveries; a synthetic event cannot drive a
commercial sprint and real customer evidence cannot drive a rehearsal; and the
canary walks all twelve states while moving no delivery, no acceptance, no
revenue and no customer.

The payment suite pins the one property that doctor exists for: LIVE_READY is
unreachable from environment presence. It needs a durable provider-origin
receipt naming a real event, verified within seven days, plus a fresh attested
KYC boundary. A stale receipt, a placeholder event id, an unattested
attestation, or an attestation with no evidence each stop short of it. PayPal
is reported as PAYPAL_RAIL_NOT_IMPLEMENTED rather than omitted, so a rail the
documents mention and the code lacks stays visible as a gap.

commits.author: Claude
commits.message:
Make the doctors runnable and the Postal evidence path real

Five lanes were writing modules when the session limit stopped them. What
survived parses and is largely complete, but four doctors had no operator
script, which is the same as not having them: nothing could run
payment-rail-doctor, first-cash-canary-packet, founder-absence-blocker-doctor
or domain-purpose-plan, so none of them had ever produced an answer.

The founder-absence doctor turned out to be the interesting one. It reports
its own software-gap list, and that list is the exit condition for this whole
mission, so it matters enormously whether the list is measured or asserted. It
is measured -- every row carries a probe evaluated against the tree -- but it
declares two probes, fileExists and sourceIncludes, and the script handed it
only one. The other silently fell back to the refusing default, so every row
resolved by a source probe reported open. The doctor was saying the work was
unfinished because nobody had given it a way to look.

Two of its probes were themselves wrong once the code they described existed.
One demanded a literal string in the Postal adapter that the adapter reaches
through an imported constant; it now checks the constant's definition and the
comparison against it, which a comment cannot satisfy. The other demanded that
three modules stay listed in the reachability classification -- but two of them
earned operator entry points when the free-first doctor began importing them,
and the ratchet then requires them to be removed from that file. A probe that
reopens a gap for improving the tree is a broken probe, not a finding.

The Postal webhook route and its migration close the evidence half of the
adapter. Verified against a real PostgreSQL rather than asserted: migration 104
applies, a redelivered webhook lands on DUPLICATE instead of becoming a second
observation, a quarantined row is excluded from reconciliation lookups, and the
append-only trigger refuses an UPDATE. The raw body and Postal's per-recipient
token are never stored -- only a digest of the bytes that were verified.

The gateway executor copied provider and transport error text verbatim into its
result. A client that echoes the request it failed on puts the Authorization
header in that string, so a timeout could write the credential into durable
task history. Its own test caught this; three sites now scrub before storing.

Also adds scripts/with-real-postgres.mjs. Roughly 180 tests about what two real
connections do to one real row have been skipping themselves in every
environment without a database server, and embedded-postgres was already a
devDependency the smoke scripts start per run. A gate that cannot run is worse
than no gate.

commits.author: Claude
commits.message:
Make LIVE outreach routing depend on receipts instead of caller booleans

selectFreeRoute's LIVE mode read four free-form booleans off providerStates.
Any caller could pass configured, active, domainAuthenticated and
providerHealthy as true and get a live route to an account that does not
exist. The registry recorded recipientCap and nothing ever compared an
audience to it, so the field was decoration. Those are the two ways this
module could have turned a research report into a send plan.

LIVE state is now derived from activation receipts: typed, secret-free
records that an external activation step hands back. A receipt carries states
and never values -- a credential anywhere in one is refused at the door by key
shape and by value shape, and the rejection itself is path-only so it cannot
leak what it caught. Receipts decay: past forty-five days a receipt yields no
live flags at all, because an observation of an account is evidence about a
moment, not a standing fact.

A receipt can only ever make routing stricter. An observed quota takes the
minimum against the researched one, so a provider reporting more headroom than
its published policy does not thereby earn it, and the cold-B2B rule takes the
stricter of registry and receipt, so a receipt claiming a provider permits cold
outreach cannot override a registry that says it does not. Receipts and
pre-derived states are mutually exclusive rather than ranked: two sources for
one truth is ambiguity, and accepting both would leave which one wins up to
argument order.

The committed artifact carries one NOT_STARTED row per reviewed provider, so
the sixteen accounts nobody has created are visible as sixteen rows rather than
as an absence. The doctor reports both numbers side by side: 75,100 messages
per thirty days is what sixteen published free-tier policies permit in
aggregate, and 0 is what this company can currently send. Proven free cold-B2B
transport across the whole reviewed pool remains zero.

Eight mutations, eight killed. Two of them -- a missing receipt and an invalid
one -- survived the first pass, because the artifact test asserted on
provider-not-active and never on the receipt state itself, so the reason codes
that name the actual problem were untested until a test named them.

The planner, the claim and the finish all existed and nothing connected them:

payment.reconciliation.tick job handler that makes it reachable.

that claims what it cannot process burns claim attempts and the repository moves

payment evidence into an uncertain state having contacted nobody.

belongs in front, governing whether to act and escalating what a pass will not
touch, while the SQL selects atomically for concurrency safety.

throws leaves the event uncertain rather than retried; two racing workers claim
once and call the provider once. Proven on a real database.

commits.author: Claude
commits.message:
Stop a forged webhook from being retried forever, and stop the receipt echoing the buyer

`/webhooks/lemonsqueezy` is the only unauthenticated route that can create money.
Its signature check is the entire boundary, and the check itself is sound -- nine
forgery shapes fail it, including a signature of a different body, one made with
another secret, the correct signature uppercased, truncated, whitespace-padded
and suffixed, and a body altered after signing. None created an order or a
revenue event. That part is left alone.

Two things around it were wrong.

A forged signature answered 500. Payment providers RETRY on 5xx, so telling Lemon
Squeezy "something went wrong on our side" about a webhook we had permanently and
correctly rejected meant it would redeliver forever -- and providers disable
endpoints that keep failing, which would cost us the deliveries that are
genuine. It is also simply false: a bad signature is the caller's problem.

Now 401, with a message saying what was wrong so the provider's own dashboard is
legible. The status travels as a property on the error, so a module below the
HTTP layer can say "this was the caller's fault" without importing an HTTP type
from the server.

And the acknowledgement echoed the whole normalized event, which carries the
provider's `attributes` verbatim -- `user_email` among them -- plus a derived
`customerEmail`. The recipient is the provider that sent it, so this was never
disclosure to a third party. But it put a buyer's address into every delivery log
and proxy on the path for no reason, and it undid the payload minimization the
durable side already does. A webhook acknowledgement needs to say "received, and
whether it was new". It now says exactly that, and a test asserts the response
contains no address-shaped value at all, on the accepted and the refused path.

One thing my own attack script got wrong, worth recording: it reported "a
correctly signed webhook is processed" as a finding because no order appeared.
The webhook was processed correctly -- the harness had never created the lead it
referenced. The permanent test creates one.

MONEY-20 removes the status that makes the refusal a 401 and MONEY-21 restores
the full-event echo. Both killed. Mutation war: 93 mutations, 93 killed.

commits.author: Claude
commits.message:
Make "cleared revenue" mean a provider cleared it, on every surface

Two surfaces disagreed about the one number this company optimizes.

`POST /api/test/unlock` marks a lead paid and writes a revenue event with no
order and no provider behind it. `reconcilePaymentRenewalTruthFromStore` -- the
canonical triple-witness truth -- correctly answered REVIEW_REQUIRED and $0 for
that lead. But `RevenueEngine.summary()` summed every positive revenue event and
called the total `clearedRevenue`, so the same fabricated payment read as $49
cleared. That figure is what the operator's dashboard shows, and it is what
`founder-command-center.mjs` publishes as `paymentTruth.cleared`.

"Cleared" is load-bearing here: it is the word separating money a provider
actually moved from money someone typed.

The rule is not new. revenue.mjs already matches revenue events to witnessing
provider orders when it reconciles refunds; summary() simply was not using it.
It does now, and an unwitnessed positive event is still reported -- under
`unwitnessedRevenue`, which is what it is. Gross is unchanged, so nothing is
hidden, only named correctly.

Verified in both directions, because the control matters more than the fix: a
real Lemon Squeezy webhook still produces clearedRevenue 49 and
PROVIDER_CLEARED_PAYMENT_PROVEN, while a test unlock produces clearedRevenue 0,
unwitnessedRevenue 49 and REVIEW_REQUIRED. A refund still nets out of gross
without being counted as an unwitnessed positive.

I changed a committed test's expectation, which deserves saying plainly.
`tests/founder-command-center.test.mjs` asserted `paymentTruth.cleared === 49`
after a test unlock -- it encoded the old meaning, and it passed for exactly the
reason the meaning was wrong. It is now strengthened rather than relaxed: it
proves a real provider payment still reaches that field, and a second test proves
a fabricated one does not. The justification is not that my change needed it to
pass; it is that the assertion contradicted the repository's own canonical
payment truth, and that contradiction is checkable independently of anything I
did.

Second fix, same route. `ALLOW_TEST_PAYMENT_UNLOCK` arms the endpoint that writes
a payment nobody made, and nothing stopped production from setting it. It is
admin-gated, so this was never remotely reachable -- but there is no version of
production where having it on is right, and an environment variable set once for
a staging run is exactly how it would arrive there. `validateStartupConfig` now
refuses to start production with it enabled, and it stays available where it is
useful.

MONEY-18 drops the order-witness requirement and MONEY-19 removes the production
guard. Both killed. Mutation war: 91 mutations, 91 killed.

commits.author: Claude
commits.message:
Extract the request handler, and stop a one-word body from producing a 500

Done under the gate built for it. tests/server-http-surface.test.mjs spawns the
real server and proved, after every step here, that it still starts and serves --
which is the only reason this refactor of the main HTTP surface was safe to make.

The change itself is small: the anonymous function passed to http.createServer is
now an exported `requestHandler`, and `server.listen` plus the SIGTERM/SIGINT
handlers are guarded behind the entry-point idiom scripts/run-tests.mjs and
scripts/mutation-war.mjs already use. Importing the module no longer binds a port.

That makes the authenticated half of the server testable at the price of a
function call rather than a socket round trip, and it immediately found something
the spawned gate could not reach:

  POST /api/campaigns with a body of `null` returned 500.

`null` is valid JSON. `parseBody` parsed it cleanly and handed it back, and the
first property access threw a TypeError. So a caller's mistake surfaced as a
server fault, and anyone could produce as many as they liked with a four-byte
body. A bare number, string, boolean or array had the same route in; `[]` did not
500 only because `[].name` is undefined, which meant an array body silently
created a campaign full of defaults.

Fixed once in `parseBody` rather than at each of the fifteen call sites: there is
one contract and every caller already assumes it. An empty body is still `{}`, a
malformed one is still 400, and a well-formed non-object is now 400 with a
message that says so. A test asserts the refusal also creates nothing on the way
through.

What the direct handler now proves that nothing did before: every admin read
answers with a valid token; a valid token does not relax method discipline; a
malformed authenticated request is never a 5xx; no error response carries a stack
trace, an internal path, or the token; every response carries the security
headers whatever its status; and an unknown path under an admin prefix is not
served by accident of prefix matching.

SRV-02 removes the non-object check and SRV-03 un-exports the handler. Both
killed, along with SRV-01. Mutation war: 89 mutations, 89 killed.

commits.message:
Gate server.mjs by running it, closing the largest coverage hole in the repository

614 lines, 87 if/switch statements, one http.createServer, and no gate executed
any of it.

The reason it stayed open is structural rather than neglect: the handler is an
inline anonymous function, and importing the module runs validateStartupConfig,
creates a store, awaits store.init() and can start a scheduler. Nothing could
reach the routing logic without a running process, so nothing did.

So the gate runs the process. It spawns the real server on loopback with a
throwaway JSON store and PROCESS_ROLE=web -- the same code production runs, minus
the scheduler -- and probes what actually matters. Every URL is 127.0.0.1 and no
external request is made.

What it now proves, none of which was proven before:

  16 admin routes each refuse an anonymous caller with 401
  each of those refuses a wrong token, a token with a suffix, a truncated token,
    and the raw token without the Bearer scheme -- 64 combinations
  the public routes are public and the list of them is short
  all five security headers reach the client on public, refused and 404
    responses alike
  a 404 carries no stack trace or internal path
  a refusal never echoes the expected token

The coverage ratchet is updated to require this rather than record it as a hole,
and it now understands that executing a module by spawning it is still executing
it -- an import closure alone reported server.mjs as uncovered and was wrong.
`worker.mjs` stays exempt on the argument entry points are usually exempt for,
and the exempt list is asserted to be one entry long so adding to it needs the
same argument made again.

This is a smoke gate, not a substitute for extracting the handler. Extraction is
still worth doing: it would make those 87 branches individually testable instead
of only reachable through a socket. But a running gate today is worth more than a
refactor of the main HTTP surface with nothing to catch a mistake in it, and this
is the net that refactor should now be done under. That ordering was the whole
judgement here.

Two harness gaps fixed on the way: the mutation sandbox did not copy server.mjs
or worker.mjs, so a mutation of either could not have meant anything. SRV-01
deletes the x-content-type-options header from the base set and is killed.

commits.message:
Gate the admin health route, and record the server.mjs coverage hole as a hole

Extending the coverage subtraction from `src` to `api` found the operator's only
window into system health, executed by no gate. Its bearer check is the only
thing between the internet and a map of the system: sender pause and bounce
state, outbound volume, queue and dead-letter depth, database capacity, egress
state, and the billing backlog.

One real finding, and it needs an honest severity. `equalBearer` coerced with
`String(header||'')`, so an object with a `toString` returning the right bearer
was admitted. That is NOT a live bypass -- over HTTP a header is only a string or
an array of strings, and an attacker cannot supply an object. It is fixed because
the coercion was doing work nobody asked for, and because
src/agent-mesh-cron-boundary.mjs already had the right shape one file over:
normalize to a string or empty, and refuse a non-string outright rather than by
accident. A single-element array is still accepted, the way that boundary accepts
it; several values are not.

The route otherwise held: configuration is checked before the secret, so an
unconfigured route cannot be used to learn whether the secret was wrong; a failing
read is 503 and never a healthy matrix; the driver's error text and internal host
do not reach the response; and the authorized response carries aggregate
telemetry with no address in it.

My second reported finding was my own test being wrong. A lowercase `get` is
served, and that is deliberate -- the method is uppercased before comparison,
consistently with the cron boundary. Pinned as a choice rather than left to look
like an oversight.

And one finding I am not fixing in this commit, recorded rather than dressed up:

  server.mjs is 614 lines with 87 if/switch statements behind one
  http.createServer, and no gate executes any of it.

That is the largest remaining coverage hole here. The handler is an inline
anonymous function and `server.listen()` runs at module scope, so nothing can
reach it without binding a port -- which explains why it is untested and is not a
reason to leave it that way. Extracting the handler behind an exported factory is
a real refactor of the main HTTP surface with no gate to catch a mistake, which
is exactly the problem, so it gets its own change with its tests written
alongside rather than being rushed in behind this one.

The ratchet records the measured branch count as a ceiling, explicitly not a
target, so the hole cannot quietly deepen while the fix is pending. worker.mjs
is separately asserted to be what entry points are usually exempt for: 60 lines,
3 branches, wiring.

ADMIN-01 restores the loose coercion, ADMIN-02 removes the configuration check.
Both killed. Mutation war: 86 mutations, 86 killed.

commits.author: Claude
commits.message:
Close the two production paths no gate executed, and ratchet the gap shut

The reachability ratchet answers "can anything call this module?". The question
underneath it -- "does anything CHECK it?" -- had never been asked.

Taking the closure of everything the gates import and subtracting it from the
production-reachable set found exactly two modules that a live route reaches and
no gate runs:

  src/database-hygiene-repository.mjs   DELETES rows on a weekly cron
  src/discovery-runner.mjs              decides whether discovery may run at all

That combination has already cost this repository once. The browser crawler
shipped a ReferenceError on every call because its only real gate had been
written off as blocked; syntax parsed it, the deterministic suite did not cover
it, and the pool's own unit tests passed because they mock the browser.

A DELETE on a schedule is the worst thing to leave in that set. Not because the
code was wrong -- it survived every attack unchanged -- but because nothing would
have noticed if it stopped being right.

Against a real database, the hygiene path holds: an unexpired cache row survives,
an expired row written today survives the updated_at guard, READY and CLAIMED
staged content survive while only terminal content past retention is taken, a
400-day-old payment_classification receipt is untouched, batch size is clamped in
both directions, and a retention value that is not a number fails the run rather
than guessing a cutoff. At the route, MAINTENANCE_ENABLED absent, "false", "1"
and "yes" all delete nothing, and a wrong secret, a missing schedule header and a
POST delete nothing even with maintenance enabled.

Two of my own errors are worth recording. My throwaway attack script wrapped the
audit-log insert in a catch, so its "money survives" check passed vacuously on a
row that was never created -- the permanent test caught that by failing on a
NOT NULL column. And I asserted 401 for a missing schedule header when the
boundary correctly answers 403: a bad secret is unauthenticated, a bad schedule
is an authenticated caller asking for something the route does not serve.

The discovery runner is proven by its refusals, all of which happen before any
Overpass request: an unknown campaign, an unapproved campaign, a missing bounding
box and an exhausted daily cap each refuse, record the failure on the run, log
it, and mark the error non-retryable so a scheduler cannot retry it forever. No
option -- scheduled, limit, dryRun, an explicit bbox -- substitutes for approval.
An errored run does not burn the day's quota. A dry run is not effect-free and
the test says so plainly: it still reaches Overpass, it only declines to import.

`tests/production-coverage-ratchet.test.mjs` keeps the set empty without anyone
re-running that analysis, and asserts its own two halves are non-trivial, since a
subtraction over derived sets is easy to make vacuously true.

One harness gap fixed: the mutation sandbox copied src, tests, scripts, config
and migrations but not `api`, so no route could be mutated at all -- a mutation
naming one failed with ENOENT rather than reporting a surviving guard. Routes are
where admission and enablement checks live. HYG-01 now sabotages the cron's
enablement check, HYG-02 the updated_at guard, HYG-03 the terminal-status filter.
All killed. Mutation war: 84 mutations, 84 killed.

commits.message:
Make the deterministic gate independent of the shell it was invoked from

Found by causing it. Running `npm run test:deterministic` from a shell that had
OMNIA_V9_TEST_DATABASE_URL exported turned a green gate red:

  not ok - property run: 1000 deterministic crash/outcome/restart scenarios,
           zero duplicate external effects

The suite passes in isolation. Most database suites are not on the runner's
exclusion list; they stay in the deterministic set and skip themselves when the
URL is absent. Export it and they execute there instead, in parallel, sharing
one database -- which is the exact interference `run-real-postgres-tests.mjs`
runs serially to avoid, and says so in its own header comment.

A gate that fails for a reason unrelated to the code is the most expensive kind
of red: it costs a diagnosis every time, and it teaches people that red might
not mean anything.

The runner now drops the variable from its children's environment, so the gate
returns the same answer on a developer's machine, in CI, and in a shell that
happens to have a database configured. Verified both ways: 2808 tests, 2760
pass, 0 fail, 48 skipped, identical with and without the variable set. Real
database coverage is not lost -- that is what `npm run test:postgres-real` is
for, serially, where it belongs.

An earlier attempt at this was wrong and is worth recording. I first made the
deterministic exclusion derive from `realPostgresTestFiles()`, reasoning that
the two runners should not disagree about what a database suite is. But that
function discovers by marker -- any file mentioning the variable -- and many
`omnia-v9-*` suites mention it only to decide whether to skip one case. Using it
as an exclusion dropped roughly 128 genuinely deterministic tests from the gate,
2807 down to 2679. The marker is correct for deciding what the PostgreSQL runner
should INCLUDE and wrong for deciding what the deterministic runner should
EXCLUDE. Two build-wiring tests caught it immediately, which is what they are
for.

GATE-01 removes the deletion and is killed. Mutation war: 81 mutations, 81
killed.
