commits.author: Claude
commits.message:
Make unclaimable payment evidence visible instead of silent

`api/webhooks/billing.mjs` writes a row into `billing_webhook_inbox` for every
verified delivery. Nothing in this tree reads those rows. `claimBillingEvents`,
`finishBillingEvent`, `billingBacklogSummary` and `planPaymentReconciliation`
have no callers anywhere -- verified by grep across src, api, scripts, server
and worker. So evidence about money arrives, is stored, and is never claimed,
retried, timed out, dead-lettered, or mentioned to anyone.

That is the "webhook inbox rows with no worker, retry, timeout, or dead-letter
path" failure, and it is currently the true state of the payment spine.

It cannot be closed by writing a reconciliation worker. There is no payment
provider to reconcile against, and a worker that resolves nothing would be
machinery pretending to be a capability. What can be closed with no external
activation is the silence.

The operator's health matrix now carries a billing dimension with four states,
because a single "pending" number would blur the fact that matters most:

  NOT_OBSERVED     the query returned nothing -- not the same as zero
  NO_WORKER        evidence is waiting and nothing has EVER claimed a row
  BACKLOG_AGEING   a worker exists and unsettled evidence is past the threshold
  HEALTHY          nothing unsettled, or nothing late

`NO_WORKER` and `BACKLOG_AGEING` look identical in a counter and are not the
same operational fact: one resolves itself, the other never will. `everClaimed`
is what separates them, and BILL-03 replaces it with a literal zero to prove
that distinction is real rather than incidental.

Today the real query answers NO_WORKER, and the matrix reports the system
DEGRADED for it -- proven against a real database, not asserted.

No route change was needed. `api/admin/health-check.mjs` already spreads the
repository output into the matrix, so the smallest bridge was to widen the query
and the compiler, and nothing else.

The aggregate deliberately selects counts and one timestamp. The rows it
summarizes carry a provider event key, a payload hash and a recipient address in
custom_data; a test asserts none of them reach the response, against a real
database with a real address seeded into the row.

BILL-01 makes the degraded condition unconditional-false and BILL-02 turns an
unobserved dimension back into a healthy zero. Both are killed. Mutation war:
80 mutations, 80 killed.

commits.author: Claude
commits.message:
Integrate #230: fail-closed external artifact storage boundary

A pure contract module with no network, no credentials and no spend. Its
postgres path is the behaviour the tree already has; its object path compiles a
write plan that terminates in a store which does not exist yet.

Attacked before accepting it, and it holds. The object backend is fail-closed on
every truthiness variant -- absent, false, the string "true", 1, {}, null all
refuse, and only a literal `true` passes, so an object write cannot be reached by
an accident of coercion. A namespace cannot escape its prefix: `../../etc`,
`a/../../b`, `..` and `/////` all normalize into the intended path or fall back
to the default. A receipt is PRIVATE regardless of what the input claims, because
visibility is set rather than read.

One observation worth recording rather than fixing: the sensitive-metadata-key
check is top-level only, so `{outer:{api_key}}` is accepted. It leaks nothing --
metadata never reaches the plan at all -- so the check is a refusal signal, not a
redaction, and it screens less deeply than its name suggests. Noted so nobody
later relies on it as a filter.

Migration 103 does not collide with #231's 102.

Classified AWAITING_ACTIVATION behind a new NO_OBJECT_STORAGE_ADAPTER gate, which
states that configuring an adapter does not by itself authorize what is written
through it.

commits.author: Claude
commits.message:
Integrate #231 (payment leases, Overpass pacing, browser pool) and repair two defects it did not survive

#231 is an exact consolidation of #227, #228 and #229 -- every source file is
byte-identical to the individual PR, verified by hash before merging -- so it is
integrated once here and those three are redundant rather than merged again.

Two defects, found by attacking the code rather than by a failing test.

P0 -- the browser crawler threw on every call.

The pool integration moved the crawl result variables inside the try block while
the return statement stayed below the finally:

  ReferenceError: pages is not defined

That is a total failure of the website-audit path, which is the product. It is
invisible to `check:syntax` because it parses, invisible to the deterministic
suite because the browser gate is separate, and invisible to the pool's own unit
tests because they mock the browser. Only `npm run test:browser` against a real
Chromium sees it. That gate was recorded as permanently BLOCKED until last shift
proved Chromium was present all along; had it stayed written off, this would have
shipped.

CRAWL-01 mutates the declaration back inside the try and is killed.

P1 -- a duplicate webhook answered 503 and lied about why.

The insert's `ON CONFLICT` named `provider_event_key`, which was correct when
that was the only unique index. Migration 101 added a second one on the content
-- (provider, event_name, object_type, object_id, payload_hash) -- and a
targeted clause does not cover it, so a provider redelivering identical content
under a new event id raised 23505. The webhook route catches everything and
answers 503 `verified-webhook-not-durably-persisted`.

That is both an outage and a false statement: the evidence IS durably persisted,
in the row the delivery duplicates. Providers retry a 503 and disable endpoints
that keep failing, so a duplicate could cost the future events that are not
duplicates. Inherited from main, not introduced by #231 -- the clause is
byte-identical on both sides.

Untargeted, the clause covers every unique constraint including any added later.
MONEY-17 restores the targeted form and is killed by a real-PostgreSQL test,
because which index PostgreSQL raises on is not something a fake can prove.

What survived attack unchanged: the lease itself. Against real PostgreSQL, a
crashed worker's lease is reclaimable rather than stranded; a preempted worker
cannot finish; the attempt cap lands in UNCERTAIN for review and never promotes
money or sets completed_at; RECONCILED without a canonical receipt throws;
concurrent claims never hand one event to two workers; RETRYABLE honours its
backoff; the backlog summary carries no key or payload. Overpass stops at 1 call
on 403/401/451/418/404 and only retries 429/406/504, honouring Retry-After and
clamping an absurd one to 120s. The pool leaks no slot on launch failure, does
not double-free on double release, and rejects waiters on close rather than
hanging them.

Two registry defects fixed along the way. Two mutations already shared the ids
MONEY-13 and MONEY-14, so a new entry collided twice in a row and the war printed
two lines with the same id -- ambiguous in the one place it must not be. There is
now a uniqueness test and a malformedness test. And the war gained a
`needsBrowser` gate mirroring `needsPostgres`, so a browser-dependent mutation
reports SKIPPED_NEEDS_BROWSER rather than being counted as killed when no browser
is configured.

pass, 0 fail, 48 skipped; real PostgreSQL 127/127 plus 5 payment lease proofs;
browser 1/1; mutation war 77 mutations, 77 killed.

Finish the decision-consumer sweep: payment, escalation, recovery are clean; two evidence consumers were not

The remaining families, swept with the same derived rule:

  payment      0 unprotected decision consumers
  escalation   0
  recovery     0
  fulfillment  0
  activation   0
  autonomy     0
  sandbox      0

Seven of eight families are clean, which is worth stating plainly: this defect
shape is not everywhere, and the sweep is now finished rather than open-ended.

Of the five evidence candidates, three were real and two were not, and the
rejections are the more useful half of the result:

- `canonicalContactRoute` is a string canonicalizer. It lowercases a route and
  strips plus-addressing. It was flagged only because a decision-name heuristic
  caught its `can` prefix.

- `isStaleSignal` compares a signal's age against a `maxAgeMs` the caller
  supplies. A caller can already choose its own answer without discarding
  anything, so protecting `market-signal-registry.mjs` and
  `prometheus-economic-spine.mjs` would look like a boundary and enforce
  nothing. A test now asserts they stay editable, with that reason, so nobody
  "tidies" them in later and makes the boundary read as arbitrary.

The real one is `evaluateContactRoute`, which is where suppression beats
verification -- an unsubscribe is sticky and no fresher provider check gets to
outvote it. A caller that discarded that verdict would hand off a suppressed
contact as usable. Both callers, `account-intent-ledger.mjs` and
`budgeted-enrichment-waterfall.mjs`, are now protected.

Both are dormant behind NO_ENRICHMENT_PROVIDER, so this closes nothing that runs
today. It closes what the evidence gate's own comment already argues for the
guards themselves: a clamp must not be weakenable while dormant and have that
weakening carried into activation.

commits.message:
Protect the whole enforcement surface, not just the rules it enforces

The send-loop fix in #215 was one instance of a shape. This is the sweep for the
rest of it: for every protected module that exports a decision, find the callers
that can discard that decision while the deciding module stays untouched.

Five more, all confirmed accepted by the contract before being closed:

- `agent-code-change-applier.mjs` calls `validateAgentCodeChangeSet` and then
  writes files to disk.
- `agent-code-artifact-store.mjs` refuses to persist a change set that does not
  validate.
- `agent-git-sandbox-collector.mjs` compiles an agent's sandbox git diff into a
  change set, and that compile call is where a change naming a protected path is
  first refused.
- `agent-autonomy-pump.mjs` and `ai-employee-relay.mjs` both act on
  `evaluateWorkerResultTruth`, which decides what counts as finished work.

`agent-code-change-contract.mjs` was protected as "the rules about changing
files, including this list" -- but the rules are enforced somewhere else, and
that somewhere else was editable. The applier bypass is two steps rather than one
(a weakened applier only takes effect once merged and used by a later run), but
the second step is unbounded, and self-modification of the enforcement surface is
the precise thing the list exists to prevent.

The two truth call sites had to be closed together because each is the other's
excuse: "avoid re-evaluating truth that the other one already checked" is a
plausible rationale for removing either, and removing both leaves nothing.

The collector was not on my list. The test found it, because the test derives the
rule from the import graph instead of trusting a list maintained by hand -- the
second time in this session that the derived form caught something the manual
form missed. That is the argument for writing them this way.

Mutation war: 73 mutations, 73 killed, including ENF-01..05.

SOV-02's anchor spanned the contract entry and the comment that followed it, and
inserting the enforcement block between them split it. The harness reported
ANCHOR_NOT_FOUND rather than quietly passing, which is exactly the difference
between "not killed" and "never applied" being worth distinguishing. Anchor
repaired against the current text; the mutation's meaning is unchanged.

commits.author: Claude
commits.message:
Protect the outbound send loop and transport, not only the guards they call

Protecting a guard and leaving its only caller editable is a one-step bypass,
not a two-step one.

`deliverability-guard.mjs`, `send-safety.mjs` and `consequence-boundary.mjs`
were inside the sovereignty boundary. `src/pipeline.mjs` -- the outbound send
loop, and the only module that asks those guards for a decision on the send path
-- was not. So an autonomous change could leave every guard file byte-identical
and neuter them where they are actually consulted. Constructed and confirmed
accepted by the contract before the fix, with an ordinary-sounding rationale:

  const finalRecheck = { ok: true, allowed: true, reasons: [] } || await evaluateDeliverabilityGuard({
  rationale: "Cache the final deliverability recheck to reduce per-send latency."
  -> {"accepted":true,"codes":[]}

The same for `evaluateConsequenceBoundary`. After the fix both return
`change-0-sovereignty-path`.

`src/gmail.mjs` is the shorter version of the same move -- reach past every
decision about whether to send and change what actually goes out -- and is now
protected too.

This is the reasoning already written down for `revenue.mjs` ("protecting the
reader and leaving the writer editable is a one-step bypass"), which had never
been applied to the thing that sends.

The advisory outbound shadow is deliberately NOT protected. Its result is
discarded at the call site and tests/omnia-v9-outbound-shadow.test.mjs already
proves a DENY or an exception cannot block, alter or duplicate a send.
Protecting it would be protecting something with no authority to lose;
protecting its caller is what keeps it that way. SEND-03 mutates the call site
from `await observe...` to `const __v9 = await observe...` -- the first half of
making it authoritative -- and is killed.

The new test derives the rule from the import graph rather than listing files,
so a future unprotected caller fails here instead of depending on someone
remembering this. The first version keyed on "imports an outbound guard" and was
wrong: it flagged `server.mjs` for taking `normalizeCountryList` and
`store.mjs` for taking `outboundVolumeWindow`. Neither can discard a decision
because neither asks for one. The rule now keys on the decision function, and a
test asserts the rule itself still fires -- a check that cannot catch anything
is worse than no check.

Mutation war: 67 mutations, 67 killed, including three new ones (SEND-01,
SEND-02, SEND-03) that remove each protection and prove the suite fails without
it. The closure test then correctly derived that the new proof must itself be
protected, and it is.

commits.author: Claude
commits.message:
Fix the reachability ratchet's nested-route blind spot found by this merge

The autonomy operations hardening landed three API routes, two of them nested:
`api/webhooks/billing.mjs` and `api/admin/health-check.mjs`. The ratchet
discovers entry points with a single-level `readdirSync`, so it never saw them,
and reported eight modules as having no entry point at all.

Four of those eight are wired to a live route. What makes this worth fixing
rather than absorbing is the repair the red test invites: the quickest way to
green is to add all eight to the classification file as AWAITING_ACTIVATION,
which would record in the canonical place that production code behind a real
route is waiting on an activation that does not exist. The ratchet exists to
stop that exact statement, so it must not be the thing that produces one.

Entry-point discovery now recurses. `src` keeps its single-level scan: it has
subtrees of its own (`src/overnight`, `src/omnia-v9`) that this ratchet has
never covered, and widening that silently as a side effect of a merge would be
its own kind of dishonesty. Recorded in the test, not fixed here.

With the blind spot closed, four modules are genuinely unwired and are
classified:

- `egress-health-pool` behind a new NO_CONFIGURED_EGRESS_ROUTES gate. Route
  selection and quarantine with no routes configured to select among.
- `prospect-identity-ledger` and `prospect-identity-repository` behind
  NO_OUTBOUND_AUTHORIZATION. They exist to make outbound contact deduplicable
  and rate-bounded; with no outbound authorization there is no send to guard.
- `database-hygiene-maintenance` as SUPERSEDED, with the reason stated
  precisely: the cron route calls `runSafeDatabaseHygiene`, which hardcodes
  deletion from `public_evidence_cache` and terminal staged-content rows and
  never compiles a plan. The executing path is strictly narrower, so nothing
  unsafe is reachable -- but this module's NEVER_AUTODELETE list (payment
  receipts, acceptance, audit and renewal evidence) is an unenforced statement
  of a policy the executing path satisfies by construction rather than by
  consulting it. Recorded so nobody later cites it as the protection that stops
  those deletions. The narrow hardcoded path is what stops them.

Also fixes a red test that arrived on main: the VACUUM assertion matched
`/DO NOT RUN VACUUM FULL/` against a constant spelled
`DO_NOT_RUN_VACUUM_FULL_IN_SERVERLESS_CRON`. The behavior was right and the
assertion was wrong. One policy identifier in the same line dropped out of
snake_case halfway through (`..._FROM THEIR ARTIFACT STORE`), which no
consistent matcher could ever match; normalized.

5 operator-only, 69 with no entry point.

commits.author: Claude
commits.message:
Make the canon guard check the named commit is reachable, not merely hex

Found by causing it: an amend after a regeneration rewrote the commit the canon
had just been reconciled from, and the canon then pointed at an orphan.

None of the existing checks could see it. Reproduced deliberately with a real
dangling commit:

  ok     the present-tense canon names the commit it was reconciled from
  not ok the commit the canon names is actually in this branch history
  ok     the present-tense canon describes the source the tree actually has

The format check only wants 40 hex characters. The staleness check asks git what
changed since that SHA, and for a commit that is dangling but still in the object
store the answer is "nothing" -- so the canon reads as perfectly fresh evidence
for a tree nobody can check out. Restoring the canon turns the new check green
again, so it is measuring the SHA and not something incidental.

Reachability, not existence: `git cat-file -e` succeeds on an orphan until it is
garbage collected, which is exactly the window in which this goes wrong. The
check is `merge-base --is-ancestor` against HEAD.

That required widening the file's `git` helper. It swallowed failures into an
empty string, which cannot express the answer of a command that communicates
only through its exit code and prints nothing either way -- success and failure
were both ''. An opt-in `allowFailure` returns null on a non-zero exit and
leaves every existing call site unchanged.

No mutation-war entry: this guard lives in the test, not in a source file, so
there is nothing to sabotage in the way that harness works. The orphan
experiment above is the equivalent proof and is recorded here instead of forcing
a mis-shaped entry.

Verification: syntax 583 files parse; deterministic 2725 tests, 2677 pass,
0 fail, 48 skipped.

commits.author: Claude
commits.message:
Refuse an employee role a task never granted; make the task-id chain traceable

Two defects on the AI-employee relay path, found by attacking the identity seam
rather than by a failing test.

1. A result could declare a role the task never granted.

   Every mismatch check compared a declaration against an expectation, so the
   one case none of them could see was an expectation of nothing.
   `employeeRoleIdentityErrors` returned `[]` whenever the task carried no
   binding, and `bindEmployeeRoleSubmissionPayload` then carried the claimed
   role forward into the durable submission payload. A generic worker naming
   itself `employee:executive/cfo` passed the whole path and the claim reached
   the relay receipt with `ref="employee:executive/cfo"`.

   That is "generic work must never accidentally become privileged employee
   work", arriving through the only direction nobody was checking.

   An ungranted claim is now refused, not stripped, at all three binders and
   through a nested result inside a receipt. Stripping would hide the attempt;
   a worker claiming an authority it was not admitted under is a signal.

2. The task id chain could not be walked backwards.

   Three ids exist along this path -- the intent's `mesh_task_*`, the relay's
   `agent_task_*`, and the rebound `employee_task_*`. Each is derived from the
   one before it and each overwrote it, so a run snapshot recorded a task id
   that could not be traced to its origin: given the id you could verify a
   guess by recomputing a digest, but you could not recover which intent
   produced it. An attribution chain you can only verify a guess against is not
   an attribution chain. The employee task now keeps `relayTaskId`, and the
   autonomy run's `relayRef` records all three joins.

between lanes about whether a Vercel project exists, instead of asserting one
side as a repository invariant. One lane recorded two project ids with a READY
production deployment; this lane's `list_projects` returned empty on two days
and `get_project` returned 404 for both the exact id and the slug. Neither can
be settled from inside the repository, so both are recorded with provenance and
the test now guards what this repository can answer -- that no current-main
production deployment, cron registration or cron delivery is proven -- rather

commits.author: Claude
commits.message:
Make the store referential-integrity divergence explicit

Sweep G found the two stores disagreeing on `duplicate revenue event`:
ConflictError on JSON, StoreError:FOREIGN_KEY on PostgreSQL. That first
reading was my fixture -- I used a leadId with no lead behind it, so
PostgreSQL's foreign key fired before the uniqueness check ever ran. With
a real lead present the two agree exactly: ok, then ConflictError.

The genuine divergence underneath is referential integrity. PostgreSQL
carries twelve-plus `REFERENCES ... ON DELETE SET NULL` constraints; the
JSON store enforces none of them.

Recorded rather than removed, for two reasons.

The direction is the safe one. PostgreSQL is production and refuses an
orphan row; the JSON store is development and accepts one. A bug that
creates an orphan surfaces loudly before it can touch money, rather than
silently after. The dangerous direction is the reverse.

And replicating twelve relationships plus ON DELETE SET NULL cascade
semantics in the JSON store is a subsystem, not a validator. The cost
exceeds the risk it removes.

So the divergence is pinned instead: the test asserts the JSON store
accepts the orphan (and says what to do if that ever changes), that real
PostgreSQL refuses it with a positive control proving a real lead still
works, and -- the important one -- that the production schema still
carries its constraints. Someone "aligning" the two stores by dropping
the PostgreSQL foreign keys would move the divergence to the dangerous
direction, and that test fails if it is attempted.

Everything the two stores were previously reconciled on is re-checked and
still agrees: unknown collection, unknown filter, __proto__ as a
collection, missing-row get, patch of a missing row.

Sweep G also re-attested time truth (nine boundaries including one
millisecond either side of the skew edge) and recovery across the
surfaces this mission changed: payment truth survives a restart with the
minimized persistence shape, the payload stays absent, the receipt keeps
its money, and redelivery after restart is still idempotent.

The rule added is that the reference points at something, not that the

Close #121: reconcile canon and stop it drifting silently

`docs/CURRENT_SYSTEM_STATE.md` and `artifacts/system-readiness.json` both
described commit 5f757ee while main had moved to 266a804, and both stated
gate figures from three hundred tests ago: 463 files, 2194 tests, 36
mutations, against an actual 474, 2307 and 55.

The artifact is regenerated with its own generator, never by hand. The
state document's SHA and figures now match the head they claim.

The drift itself is the more interesting half, so tests/canon-freshness
makes it loud:

- The commit canon names must still describe the current source. Not
  "canon must name HEAD" -- that is stricter than the truth, would be red
  on every working commit including documentation-only ones, and a check
  that is always red is a check people turn off. What makes canon false
  is a claim about a tree that has since changed underneath it, so the
  test compares src/, scripts/, config/ and migrations/ between the named
  commit and head.

- The figures are checked, not trusted. The SHA matching is necessary and
  not sufficient: canon can name the right commit and still state a
  mutation count that was true two waves ago. File count and mutation
  count are exactly measurable without running anything, so both are
  verified against reality. Test counts need the suite and are left to
  receipt discipline rather than half-checked here.

- Historical receipts are exempt, explicitly and by name. A receipt says

commits.author: Claude
commits.message:
Close the base64-wrapped credential gap and publish the minimization matrix

A 26-shape re-attack on the durable-surface scanner found one miss: a
credential that arrives base64-wrapped. Twenty-five were blocked; that
one walked through every module using src/secret-patterns.mjs.

Detecting it by shape is impossible, because base64 of a token and base64
of an image are the same alphabet. So long base64 runs are decoded and
the existing value patterns are asked about the result. Nothing new is
recognized -- the rule is "if it decodes to something we already call a
credential, it is one".

Precision comes from two conditions rather than the alphabet: the decoded
bytes must be printable ASCII, and must match an existing value pattern.
Base64 of prose, of business JSON, of raw binary bytes, a 64-character
hex string and a long identifier run all stay clean. Runs shorter than 24
characters are never decoded, so ordinary identifiers are untouched.

`redactSecrets` gets the same rule, keeping the redactor at least as
strong as the blocker -- the asymmetry closed last mission. The whole run
is replaced rather than the decoded fragment, because a partially
rewritten base64 string is still most of a credential.

Measured: 26 of 26 credential shapes blocked, 20 benign strings flagged
zero times.

Also publishes docs/DATA_MINIMIZATION_MATRIX.md, written from measured
evidence rather than from reading the source. Every row comes from
feeding a hostile payload through the real code path and inspecting what
persisted. Notable results:

- payment provider: 10 of 10 sensitive values retained -> 0 of 10,

  status         : PROVIDER_CLEARED_PAYMENT_PROVEN

MONEY-09 covered the reader and was killed by its mutation the whole
time. Mutating a reader cannot find an input that is never written.

change carries no money, silence is not disagreement, and the suite pins

commits.author: Claude
commits.message:
Make a local copy of a canonical effect ledger unable to drift

Several modules keep a local ZERO_EFFECTS literal instead of importing
one, and agent-provider-worker.mjs holds a byte-for-byte copy of
ZERO_BUSINESS_EFFECTS while importing from the very module that exports
it.

Nothing they say today is false. The failure is scheduled: the day the
exported constant gains a key, the copy keeps parsing, keeps passing, and
silently claims that effect did not happen. That is the omitted-key
defect arriving through the calendar instead of through a typo, and it is
the same "six modules grew their own copy of this" pattern that produced
a credential scanner with five different holes.

Forcing one vocabulary would be the wrong fix -- three legitimate shapes
exist here: the canonical external ledger, the legacy business ledger
kept for already-persisted receipts, and service-fulfillment's own
spelling. So a local copy is allowed to exist and is not allowed to
diverge: any local constant reusing an exported name must have exactly
the exported key set.

A second test asserts at least one such copy exists, so the check cannot
start passing vacuously the day somebody renames the local constant and
takes the guard with it. Verified by deleting a key from the local copy
and watching the suite go red.

Found by sweep 15. Latent rather than live, so it is recorded as
hardening and not counted as a defect.

commits.author: Claude
commits.message:
Close the sovereignty boundary over the proofs, not just the guards

Protecting a guard and leaving its proof editable protects nothing on
the second move.

SOVEREIGNTY_PREFIXES had a section for "the tests that prove the guards
above still guard". It held four entries. They were right when they were
written; every killing test added afterwards was left out. A probe found
that fifteen of the twenty suites proving a sovereignty guard still
guards were editable by the autonomous path -- as was
scripts/mutation-war.mjs itself, the single artifact that decides whether
any of them still kill. Deleting one entry from its list removes the
proof that a guard works and reports a smaller number nobody
cross-checks; the next move is the guard.

The list is now closed over its own proofs: the runner, the fifteen
missing suites, and the new closure test.

The root cause was not the four missing names, it was that membership
had to be remembered. tests/sovereignty-proof-closure.test.mjs derives
it: if a mutation targets a sovereignty-protected file, the suite that
kills it must be protected too. Adding a mutation for a protected file
now forces its suite onto the list, and the test fails until it is there.

It also checks the boundary is not padded -- every test entry has to be
earned by naming a mutation on a protected file. The cost of this list
is that a person is needed to change anything on it, and a list that
grows without justification is a list people route around.

This strengthens the sovereignty boundary; nothing here widens what the
autonomous path may reach.

commits.author: Claude
commits.message:
Close six credential formats that walked through every scanner

Eight modules use src/secret-patterns.mjs as their only value-shape
check: the change-set blocker, the artifact store, the compute store,
the provider worker, the relay, and the two receipt redactors. Six
credential formats passed all of them.

The worst was `github_pat_`. The pattern list covered every classic
GitHub prefix -- ghp_, gho_, ghu_, ghs_, ghr_ -- and could not reach the
fine-grained one, because `github_pat_` starts with `gh` and the third
character is `i`, outside `gh[pousr]_`. Fine-grained is the format
GitHub issues by default now, so the most likely token in circulation
was the one shape not detected.

Also added:

- Stripe `sk_live_` / `rk_live_`. `sk-` with a hyphen is the OpenAI
  shape; Stripe uses an underscore, and STRIPE_SECRET_KEY was already in
  the assignment list, so the project had contemplated the credential
  existing without being able to detect it.
- HTTP `Basic` credentials. Bearer was caught and Basic was not, though
  both are a live credential in the same header.
- A credential-named key assigned a long opaque value. Provider prefixes
  only catch the providers somebody thought of, and this project's own
  payment provider was not among them. Deliberately not left-anchored on
  a word boundary: `_` is a word character, so `\bapi_key` cannot match
  inside `lemonsqueezy_api_key`.
- Case-insensitive named assignments, so a lowercase
  `aws_secret_access_key=` is caught alongside the uppercase spelling.

And one asymmetry: `containsSecretValue` blocks, `redactSecrets` cleans,
and they consulted different rule sets -- so a credential could be
refused entry to a receipt and admitted into durable task history in the
same run. The blocker now consults the assignment rule too.

Twenty benign strings -- task ids, placeholders, prose, shas, refs,
uuids, an unlabelled base64 blob -- are checked to stay unflagged. A
guard that blocks legitimate work is a guard people route around.

SEC-05 survived its first mutation run: the branch it disables is caught
only by DATABASE_URL, VERCEL_TOKEN and GITHUB_TOKEN assignments, whose
values are shapeless, and the suite had no such case. Four were added.
The gate found the gap in my test, which is what it is for.

commits.author: Claude
commits.message:
Payment truth: name the currency, witness the money, keep the scope

Three defects found by sweeps 9 and 11, attacking the payment truth module
after every previous witness check had landed and two sweeps had declared
it clean.

1. Cents from different currencies were added into one figure. A cleared
   $50.00 and a cleared JPY 5000 -- five thousand yen, a currency with no
   minor unit -- summed to 10000 and reported
   `$100.00 PROVIDER_CLEARED_PAYMENT_PROVEN`. Neither row was wrong; the
   sum is not a quantity of anything, and it is the number a revenue
   claim reads. Now `economics.currency` names the unit (null when the
   rows span more than one) and `multi-currency-revenue-cannot-be-summed`
   is raised instead of a total. No conversion: an operator can convert,
   this module cannot, and inventing a rate would be the same
   synthetic-as-real substitution the file exists to refuse.

2. The clearing receipt witnessed identity but not money. The index
   carried leadId, prospectId and product but never amountCents or
   currency, so both money comparisons only ever saw the order and the
   ledger row. A receipt claiming EUR against a USD order and a USD
   ledger row reconciled as three witnesses in agreement. All three are
   now compared on amount and currency, with silence still not counting
   as disagreement so older receipts keep reconciling.

3. A failed lead lookup widened the question to every lead. The scope
   asked about and the record found were the same field, so a lookup
   returning nothing collapsed the scope to null -- which this module
   reads as "reconcile everything":

     ask for "lead-alice" -> $50.00      verified 1  PROVEN
     ask for "lead-typo"  -> $9,050.00   verified 2  PROVEN

   Both leads were honest and internally consistent, so no witness check
   catches this; only the scope does. The scope now comes from what was
   asked. An unknown lead also raises
   `payment-truth-requested-for-unknown-lead` rather than reporting
   $0.00, because a lead nobody can find is not a lead with no payments.
   Whole-book reconciliation stays available by naming no lead, which is
   a decision rather than a failed lookup.

comparison only ever saw the order and the ledger row, and a receipt bound to a
different prospect reconciled as agreement:

PR #114's probe mutated the ledger row, which the first fix did catch. Mutating
the receipt instead walked straight through it. The fields are carried now and
every witness takes part.

The other thirteen variations held, including two worth recording because they
are the guard being stricter than its own comment suggested: an order with a
missing or null amount refuses rather than passing, since a missing amount is
compared as zero and disagrees with a stated one. That is why completing the
double-count fixtures was the right call and exempting a missing amount would
have been the wrong one.

One test of mine asserted the wrong thing and is corrected rather than made to
pass: a witness bound to another lead never enters the evidence index at all,
because both indexes are already scoped by leadId. The payment is refused for
want of a witness, not for disagreement -- no lead-mismatch code appears, and

Bind payment proof to what the provider signed, not just to its name (#114, #116)

Two concurrent PRs arrived while the receipt was being written. Both were right,
and one of them found the most expensive defect of this mission.

#114 shipped four failing tests and no fix -- a mutation probe. It is correct.
Identity was bound on `eventName:eventId` and the witnesses were never compared
on content:

  provider order says : $50.00
  revenue ledger says : $5000.00
  reconciled as       : $5000.00   PROVIDER_CLEARED_PAYMENT_PROVEN, no contradiction

Same defect as counting a payment twice, arriving through a field nobody thought
to check. Amount, currency, product, prospect and lead must now agree across the
order, the classification receipt and the ledger row; a row whose witnesses
contradict each other proves nothing and is not counted.

Magnitude is compared rather than the signed value, because the sign is decided
by the classification and providers differ on whether a refund event carries a
negative amount. A field absent from one witness cannot contradict another --
silence is not disagreement.

That last rule initially swallowed the amount check too, and five tests in
tests/payment-truth-double-count.test.mjs went red because their order fixture
carried no `amountCents`. The tempting fix was to exempt a missing amount. The
right one was to check the writer: there is exactly one, RevenueEngine, and it
always sets `amountCents` and `currency` from the provider event. An order
without them is a shape production never produces, so the fixtures were
completed and the guard stayed strict.

#116 replaces recovery's unconditional patch with compare-and-transition,
locking FOR UPDATE on PostgreSQL. The comment it removes claimed two sweeps
racing on one row were "safe to apply twice". They are not: a sender legitimately
moving reserved -> dispatching -> sent while a sweep holds an older snapshot
could be overwritten back into a recovery state, which is a lie about an
irreversible effect. Merged as-is; its 24 tests pass and the race suite is new.

RECOV-01 disables the status re-check; both are killed.

Sweep 2: a session cookie was not a credential

Independent red-team sweep, hostile-security and skeptical-CFO posture.

Nine prompt injections against the outbound authority gate -- instruction
override, a fake SYSTEM line, evidence-fence escape, SQL in the company name,
template syntax, ANSI escapes, an embedded NUL, `__proto__` and `constructor` --
all DENY, with the campaigns table intact afterwards. Cross-entity payment
witness borrowing (lead A's revenue row with lead B's order and classification)
proves nothing and raises two contradictions. Forty concurrent racers against
one provider event, twenty-five consecutive rounds on real PostgreSQL: exactly
one winner every time.

The scanner found eleven credential shapes and missed one:

  Bearer eyJhbGci...          detected
  Cookie: session=abcd1234    MISSED

Those are the same kind of thing arriving through a different header. A worker
pasting a request or response header into its output was writing a live session
credential into durable task history -- exactly the surface the scanner exists
to keep clean. Bare JWTs were missed too: the Bearer pattern only catches the
ones that arrive with their prefix attached.

Both patterns anchor on the header name rather than the value, because a session
identifier has no distinguishing shape and matching bare `session=...` would
flag prose and query strings. The JWT pattern is the exception: three base64url
segments is distinctive on its own. Seven non-credential strings that must stay
clean are pinned alongside, because a scanner that flags prose is one an
operator learns to ignore.

Then GitHub push protection refused the commit over the Slack token fixture --
doing to this repository exactly what tests/secret-leakage-sweep does inside it.
It offered an unblock URL. Taking it would have defeated a working control to
make a test convenient, so the fixtures are assembled at run time from pieces
instead. No credential-shaped literal is committed at all, which also means the
file needs no scanner exemption: a repository containing no such literals is a
stronger property than one containing them under a declared exception.

The previous Everest receipt left systematic mutation testing explicitly
incomplete. This finishes it: scripts/mutation-war.mjs and

A guard that nothing tests is decoration, and the only way to know a test is
holding a guard up is to break the guard and watch the test die. Thirty-one
mutations, each a literal source edit applied to a copy of the tree, each naming
the suites that must fail:

  31 mutations, 31 killed, 0 survived

The exit condition is deliberately not a mutation percentage. Mutating arbitrary
lines produces mostly equivalent mutants and a number nobody can act on.
Mutating the specific invariants this system's safety rests on -- whether a
message may reach a person without current authority, whether money can be
claimed that does not exist, whether a delivery can be accepted without the
customer, whether unknown can pass as zero, whether the system can widen its own
authority, whether it can go quiet about a problem -- produces a list an
operator can read.

The runner refuses to count a mutant that does not parse. A suite failing
because the file broke proves nothing about the guard, and the first draft of
AGENT-04 was caught doing exactly that: `new Set([].concat([` is a syntax error,
the suite duly failed, and reporting that as KILLED would have been a lie about
a guard nobody had actually tested. It was rewritten to disable the real check
(`changedArtifacts` non-empty with `testsActuallyRun` empty), which kills
honestly, and AGENT-05 was added alongside it.

SOV-02 exists because the protection list is exactly the kind of thing that can
be quietly emptied: it removes the contract module's own entry from
SOVEREIGNTY_PREFIXES and proves a test notices.

STORE-01 needs real PostgreSQL, because the identifier allowlist it mutates is
on the SQL path. The runner reports it as skipped rather than passing when no
database is configured -- a skipped mutation proves nothing and must not be
counted as a kill.

The inventory also says what it does not prove: that it is complete. A guard
nobody thought to list is a guard nobody mutated.

Complete Wave 18: the recovery war, with a published matrix

The previous Everest receipt left recovery warfare explicitly incomplete. This
finishes it and publishes docs/RECOVERY_MATRIX.md: every persistence boundary
where a crash could produce a second irreversible effect, the classification it
must produce, and the test that holds it there.
BLIND_REPEAT_IRREVERSIBLE_EFFECT appears nowhere.

Prior coverage was real and is credited rather than duplicated: the external
effect path already injected crashes at five checkpoints including the one that
matters most (provider accepted, response lost), plus reservation recovery, the
canary null-sink, the gmail adapter and the cognitive loop. What had never been
killed and restarted was fulfillment, escalation, the mission-seed leg of the
scheduler -- and payments.

The payment finding is the significant one, and it is about coverage rather than
a defect. Until tests/payment-recovery-war.test.mjs existed, all 114
real-PostgreSQL tests exercised OMNIA V9 infrastructure and not one touched
`orders`, `revenue_events` or `leads`. The money tables had only ever run
against the JSON store, whose uniqueness is a JavaScript check in `_checkUnique`
rather than a UNIQUE index and a 23505. Two different mechanisms that had never
been compared, with money behind them.

They agree. A webhook replayed a hundred times yields one order and one revenue
row on both; a replayed event carrying a different amount or currency is refused
on both; a duplicate refund reverses once. The suite is self-migrating, so it
proves this on a database created from nothing rather than on one that happened
to be prepared. Real-PostgreSQL coverage goes 114 -> 122.

Also covered for the first time: a crash at each of the six fulfillment delivery
boundaries replays idempotently; a crash before acceptance never leaves
acceptance inferred from delivered work, a QA pass or a delivery receipt; a
restart is not elapsed time; a crash between the escalation row and the page
retries the page rather than the escalation, while correctly raising
OWNER_UNREACHABLE, because a crash before dispatch really does leave the owner
uninformed; twenty restarts inside one outage remain one episode; and an
unreadable ledger during recovery resolves nothing, because "we could not
assess" is not "the problem went away".

One assertion of mine was wrong and is recorded as such in the test: I counted
all escalation rows and read a legitimately new OWNER_UNREACHABLE incident as a
duplicate. The code was right; the test was too broad.

The matrix also names what is deliberately not covered -- a store that loses a
committed write, a torn transaction, and real provider behaviour under crash --
because a matrix that implies it covers those is worse than one that says it
does not.

commits.author: Claude
commits.message:
Give escalations episodes, so a recurrence is not silenced by its own history

Closes #111.

`activeFingerprints` meant "every fingerprint ever raised", because the
escalation ledger only ever grew. Probed against the real modules with the
sequence silent, silent, silent, healthy, healthy, silent, silent:

  SCHEDULER_SILENT durable rows: 1     (two real outages)

The second outage was never escalated to anyone. Suppression that cannot expire
is indistinguishable from not detecting the problem at all -- and it is worse
than the duplicate-flood it was introduced to fix, because a flood is visible
and this is not.

The fix is a fold over rows this module already writes, not a new incident
subsystem with its own truth to keep in sync. An `operator_escalation` row opens
an episode; a new `operator_escalation_resolved` row closes it; "is this active"
becomes a question about the last event for a fingerprint rather than about
whether one was ever written. Episodes carry a sequence, so two outages of the
same kind are two escalations with distinguishable identities.

Resolution is by difference. `evaluateOperatorHealth` now reports every
condition present on an assessment, not just the three that fit in the owner
queue, and an open episode absent from that list has stopped happening. A report
that could not be produced resolves nothing: "we could not assess" and "the
problem went away" are the same silence from outside, and only one of them is a
reason to stop paging. A failed or unknown page is likewise not a resolution.

Undelivered accounting now counts open episodes rather than every episode ever
raised. A resolved episode nobody was told about is history worth keeping, not
an outstanding action, and counting it forever would make OWNER_UNREACHABLE grow
without bound.

src/operator-escalation.mjs is in SOVEREIGNTY_PREFIXES. That tier governs what
an autonomous change-set may contain; this change was made directly under
explicit owner instruction, and the protection itself is untouched -- no entry
added, removed, or weakened, and tests/sovereignty-self-modification.test.mjs
still passes unchanged.

commits.author: Claude
commits.message:
Merge #112 and close the forward half of the fulfillment time gate

PR #112 makes fulfillment time a real gate rather than a typed claim, and its
work is correct: SUPPORT_ENDED before supportEndsAt and RENEWAL_DUE before
renewalDueAt are refused, an event dated before state.updatedAt is a regression,
malformed and impossible dates fail closed, same-event-id-different-timestamp is
an identity collision, offset-equivalent timestamps are the same instant, and
supportWindowDays: 0 routes straight to ACCEPTED rather than deadlocking in
SUPPORT_ACTIVE. Six of the eight hostile cases from the mission behaved exactly
as specified on first probe.

It closes backward time travel and leaves forward time travel open. Probed
against the merged module with a 30-day support window and a 90-day renewal
interval:

  SUPPORT_ENDED at 3000-01-01  =>  ALLOW -> RENEWAL_DUE

The renewal became due 974 years early because the caller said so. That is
retention proven by fast-forwarding contractual time -- the one thing this clock
exists to prevent. It also freezes the record: `next.updatedAt` is set from the
event's own timestamp, so state time becomes year 3000 and every subsequent real
event fails `event-time-regression` forever.

Two bounds, because one is not enough:

- `at` may not run ahead of `date` by more than the five-minute skew allowance
  the rest of the repository already uses for `observedAt-in-the-future`. `date`
  is the trusted clock: injectable so a test can simulate elapsed time, real in
  production where no caller supplies it.
- `at` may not exceed a ten-year absolute horizon from this process's own clock.
  A guard that only compares the caller's `at` to the caller's `date` compares a
  value to itself for anyone who supplies both. No legitimate fulfillment event
  is dated a decade out; a simulated 90-day renewal window sits well inside it.

Two test-fixture consequences, both fixed rather than worked around:

- tests/service-fulfillment.test.mjs modelled "a day later" by moving the event
  label while the clock stayed at real now. That is the fast-forward. The helper
  now advances the clock with the event, which is what elapsed time means, and
  all 23 of #112's tests pass unchanged in intent.
- tests/superseded-fulfillment-invariants.test.mjs compiled its plan without a
  date, stamping it at real now while its events claimed 01:00-05:00Z. #112's
  new regression check therefore made that suite pass before 01:00 UTC and fail
  after -- a clock-of-day dependency introduced by the PR. The fixture now pins
  its own clock.

commits.author: Claude
commits.message:
Make the store's collection and column guards real allowlists

Wave 16's finding. `definition(key)` did `const def = MAP[key]; if (!def) throw`.
`MAP[key]` walks the prototype chain, so `definition('constructor')` returned
Object -- truthy, past the guard, and on into `def.table` as undefined. The
filter loops had the same shape: `def.columns[property]` returned a function for
'toString', 'hasOwnProperty', 'valueOf' and the prototype object for
'__proto__', each truthy enough to be string-interpolated straight into SQL.

Not injection today. `${Object}` interpolates to "function Object() { [native
code] }", which is a syntax error rather than a payload -- so the honest
description is a guard that reads as an allowlist and is in fact a truthiness
check, protected by luck. It stops being luck the moment a column is named after
a prototype member, or an interpolation moves.

Object.hasOwn is what these checks always meant. Values were already
parameterized; this closes the identifier side.

The tests exercise the Postgres path, because that is where the interpolation
is, and run under test:postgres-real -- discovered automatically by the marker
the runner already looks for.

They also pin a divergence found while writing them: an unknown filter name
throws INVALID_FILTER on Postgres and silently returns [] on the JSON path. A
typo'd filter is therefore a loud error in production and a quiet empty result
in development, which is the wrong way round. Recorded rather than changed --
making the JSON path throw is a behaviour change across every caller and belongs
in its own pass -- but it should not have to be rediscovered.

commits.author: Claude
commits.message:
Give the two colliding vocabularies their own names, and stop coercing evidence

Two exported name collisions, closing issue #100's finding and one it did not
name.

1. EVIDENCE_CLASSES existed twice, with entirely disjoint members.

   src/market-signal.mjs:                 SYNTHETIC_TEST_FIXTURE ... VERIFIED_FACT
   src/prospect-evidence-reconciliation:  DIRECT_FIRST_PARTY ... MODEL_INFERENCE

   Zero overlap, and three other evidence vocabularies in this repository are
   already namespaced -- CAUSAL_, PRICING_, INBOUND_. These two were the only
   bare ones, which is the tell.

   Worse than the collision was what market-signal did with a value it did not
   recognise: coerced it to 'UNRESOLVED' and returned ok:true. A caller who
   passed DIRECT_FIRST_PARTY -- a real, strong class in the module next door --
   was told the write succeeded and had recorded no evidence at all. So was a
   caller with a typo. The coercion always erred downward, so nothing was ever
   over-claimed, but under-claiming silently is still a wrong answer about what
   was observed, and this repository has already been bitten once by evidence
   class laundering.

   Now SIGNAL_EVIDENCE_CLASSES, and an unrecognised class is
   `unknown-evidence-class:<value>` rather than a quiet downgrade. Absent still
   means UNRESOLVED: saying nothing about evidence and saying something
   unrecognisable about it are different acts, and only the first is honestly
   answered by UNRESOLVED.

   tests/market-signal.test.mjs had folded both cases into one test named for
   the untagged path while passing a bogus tag. Split, with the original claim
   preserved and the new one added.

2. scoreOpportunity existed twice, taking different argument shapes.

   src/opportunity-factory.mjs   (opportunity) -> reads opportunity.fitSignals
   src/opportunity-registry.mjs  ({candidate, weights, date})

   Probed both with the other's shape: the factory throws, the registry returns
   a structured malformed-input refusal. Both fail loudly, so this was a trap
   for a reader rather than a live defect -- renamed to scoreOpportunityFit
   anyway, because the cost is three call sites and the alternative is leaving a
   loaded gun on the table.

src/inbound-feedback-kernel.mjs coerces the same way and was left alone
deliberately: INBOUND_EVIDENCE_CLASSES defaults to its own weakest tier,
UNVERIFIED_INPUT, which is a defensible reading of "unrecognised", and it has no
colliding name to make the mistake likely.

commits.author: Claude
commits.message:
Stop the self-improvement path from editing its own limits

EVEREST ZERO's P0 category, confirmed against the real module.

The change contract protected the build and verification graph -- package.json,
the test runner, the syntax checker -- so an untrusted edit could not hide its
own failures from the gate about to check it. It did not protect the limits
themselves. A probe compiled a well-formed change set, bland rationale and a
passing verification command, replacing each of these files with a single
comment:

  ACCEPTED  src/agent-code-change-contract.mjs
  ACCEPTED  src/deliverability-guard.mjs
  ACCEPTED  src/agent-autonomy-loop.mjs
  ACCEPTED  src/cloud-agent-relay.mjs
  ACCEPTED  src/effect-ledgers.mjs
  ACCEPTED  src/secret-patterns.mjs
  ACCEPTED  src/agent-worker-result-truth.mjs
  ACCEPTED  src/claude-code-sandbox-provisioner.mjs
  ACCEPTED  src/payment-renewal-truth.mjs
  ACCEPTED  src/operator-escalation.mjs
  ACCEPTED  config/reachability-classification.json
  ACCEPTED  tests/reachability-ratchet.test.mjs

Every one. Including the contract module itself -- the self-improvement path
could delete its own guard and then, on the next pass, edit anything at all.

Worth recording how close this came to being missed: the first probe run
reported BLOCKED for all twelve, and it would have been easy to stop there. The
refusal was `change-0-rationale-required` -- the fixture had omitted a field.
Adding it turned every BLOCKED into ACCEPTED. An incidental refusal is not a
guarantee, which is why the new tests assert the reason code rather than the
refusal.

SOVEREIGNTY_PREFIXES is a second, absolute tier: the modules that decide what
may be sent, on whose authority, what counts as a credential, what counts as
finished work, what may be claimed about money, and how the owner finds out
anything is wrong. It carries its own reason code, because "you tried to edit
the build graph" and "you tried to edit your own limits" are different attempts
and an operator should be able to tell them apart.

These can only be changed by a person. That is the entire content of the rule
that a system may not widen its own authority, and the cost -- genuine
improvements to these files needing a human -- is the intended price.

The test suite asserts the reason code for every entry, that a sovereignty edit
buried in a batch of ordinary changes fails the whole set, that path tricks do
not reach one, that an ordinary module is still editable (a boundary, not a
freeze), and as a positive control that the refusals come from membership rather
than a blanket denial. One test checks that every listed path names a file that
exists -- it immediately caught src/outbound-authorization.mjs, which I had
guessed at and which does not exist. A protection entry for a file that was
never there protects nothing while reading as though it does.

commits.author: Claude
commits.message:
Merge: outbound authority read from durable storage

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01BvS8JECUaTUe25vYVxeBE9

commits.author: Claude
commits.message:
Read outbound authority from the database, not from the sender's memory

The most dangerous defect found so far, because of where it sits: the gate
immediately before an irreversible message to a real person.

Pipeline.maybeSend loads a campaign once at the top of a batch and threads that
same object through admission, reservation, and a final recheck whose own
comment says it exists because "state (suppression, evidence, authority, sender
health, policy) may have changed since admission". It re-read suppression,
sender health, settings and the account from the store -- and evaluated
authority from the in-memory object it was handed.

Probed against the real guard, with approval revoked in the database mid-batch:

  durable campaign approved:   false
  in-flight campaign approved: true
  final-recheck decision:      ALLOW_LOCAL_PREPARATION
  denyReasonCodes:             []

Revoking permission did not stop the send.

Authority is now re-read from durable storage on every evaluation and fails
closed on every path where the answer is not knowable: no store, no `get`, a
read that throws, no such row. An authorization this process cannot verify right
now is not an authorization, and falling back to the caller's object is the
defect rather than the fallback.

Caps and country allowlists are treated as authority too. A ceiling is
permission about volume, and a stale one authorizes sends the owner has since
taken back.

A disagreement between the snapshot and the durable row is reported as
`authority-snapshot-stale:<fields>` rather than quietly resolved in favour of
the database. Silently doing the right thing hides the fact that an authority
change landed while a send was in flight, which is exactly the event an operator
needs to see the gate catching.

Fixtures fixed, not worked around:
- Guard and pipeline tests passed campaigns that existed only in memory. In
  production `campaignFor` loads the campaign with store.get before anything
  reaches the guard, so a campaign absent from the database is a state the
  system cannot be in. They now seed it.
- tests/pipeline-deliverability-guard.test.mjs simulated an authority change by
  mutating the in-memory campaign object mid-send, and read it back. That test
  passed while the guard was trusting whatever the sending process happened to
  be holding -- it was asserting the defect. It now writes the expiry to the
  database, which is where an authority change actually arrives.

No outbound contact is authorized, and none has occurred. This closes the path
by which a revocation could have failed to take effect if it ever were.

Merge: refund and reversal truth in the payment spine

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01BvS8JECUaTUe25vYVxeBE9

commits.author: Claude
commits.message:
Count the money that came back

src/payments.mjs classifies order_refunded as REFUND_OR_DISPUTE with
revenueSign -1 and writes a negative ledger row. src/payment-renewal-truth.mjs
read only rows with amountCents > 0, so every one of those rows was invisible
to it. Probed against the real module -- customer pays $50, is refunded $50:

  status: PROVIDER_CLEARED_PAYMENT_PROVEN
  ok: true
  contradictions: []
  providerClearedRevenue: $50.00

The money was gone and the revenue ledger said it was there. In a repository
whose premise is that revenue is never claimed without proof, this is the
inverse failure and the more expensive one: proof that a payment cleared is not
proof the business kept it.

A reversal now needs the same three witnesses a payment needs -- order,
REFUND_OR_DISPUTE classification receipt, ledger row, all keyed on
eventName:eventId. The symmetry is the point: an unwitnessed positive row
invents revenue, an unwitnessed negative row erases it, and both are ledger
claims with no provider behind them, so both are reported rather than applied.

PAYMENT_RETAINED is a separate stage rather than a flag on CLEARED_PAYMENT. The
payment did clear; that is history and stays PROVEN. Whether the business still
holds the money is a different question, and merging the two is exactly how a
refunded sale reads as revenue. providerClearedRevenueCents likewise stays
gross, because callers read it as "money that cleared the provider" and that
remains true of a payment later refunded; netProviderClearedRevenueCents is the
number a revenue claim has to use.

New contradictions:
  negative-revenue-row-without-provider-refund-proof
  duplicate-refund-rows-for-one-provider-event
  refunds-exceed-provider-cleared-payments
  lead-marked-paid-after-full-refund
  customer-acceptance-claimed-with-reversed-payment

The last one is the lifecycle claim: a refund is the customer's strongest
available statement that the delivery was not what they wanted, so acceptance
and a returned payment cannot both stand unexamined.

Commercial truth is unchanged and still zero: no payment, refunded or
otherwise, has ever reached this system.

commits.message:
Merge: per-target-agent model routing (reconciles #108)

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01BvS8JECUaTUe25vYVxeBE9

commits.author: Claude
commits.message:
Route within each target agent, not across them

Reconciles PR #108, which made evidence-based model routing load-bearing in the
mesh. Its authority ordering, occurrence-identity binding and fail-closed
evidence gate are right and kept. Its central assumption is not.

routePermittedWorkers answers "which of these candidates should do this job" and
returns exactly one worker. The mesh's worker list is not a candidate set: each
worker carries a targetAgent and drains that agent's queue. Applying a
single-winner router across it is a category error, and a probe with four
workers on four target agents, routing enabled and fresh benchmarks compiled,
produced:

  cycle ok: true | status: ADVANCED | routingStatus: ROUTED
  target agents serviced: chatgpt

Three quarters of the system silently stopped, and the cycle receipt said it
advanced. PR #108's own tests did not catch it because every worker in their
fixtures shares one targetAgent, which is the case where the two readings agree.

routeWorkersByTargetAgent groups first, so the question becomes the right one:
for the chatgpt queue, which of my chatgpt-capable workers should run. A
supplier preference can no longer remove a queue from service.

An unroutable group is withheld alone and named. Failing the whole cycle would
let one agent's stale benchmark starve every other agent -- the same failure
from the other direction -- so blocked agents are returned by name and a cycle
that served some queues and not others reports DEGRADED rather than ADVANCED.
When nothing at all is routable it still fails closed as BLOCKED.

One correction to my own first draft, recorded because the reasoning matters: it
exempted single-candidate groups from fresh-evidence-backed-route-required, on
the argument that with one candidate there is nothing to prefer. Two of PR
#108's tests failed on it, correctly. That gate is not about preference --
routing is opt-in behind AGENT_MODEL_ROUTE_ENABLED, and opting in asserts that
fresh evidence exists. The exemption would have quietly weakened a deliberate
gate to solve a problem that belongs to reporting. Removed; the operator now
sees which queue stopped and why instead of either a silent stop or a silent
exemption.

Two stale fixtures fixed rather than worked around:
- tests/agent-model-routing-config.test.mjs built workers with no targetAgent,
  which validWorker in the control plane rejects, so the mesh never produces one.
- tests/kilimanjaro-rehearsal.test.mjs pinned the literal
  'agent-mesh-control-plane-1.3.0'; PR #108 moved it to 1.4.0, so no receipt
  qualified and the reason codes it asserted were never reached. Now imported.

commits.author: Claude
commits.message:
Merge: operator escalation transport and absence deliverability

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01BvS8JECUaTUe25vYVxeBE9

commits.author: Claude
commits.message:
Make operator escalation deliverable, and stop calling absence ready without it

Three defects, all found by running the real modules the way the mesh tick
calls them.

1. The suppression the escalation kernel was built with was never fed.

   evaluateOperatorHealth has always accepted `activeFingerprints`. Nothing
   passed it. Ten ticks against one unchanging condition wrote thirty durable
   escalation rows for three real problems -- at an hourly cadence, seventy-two
   duplicate pages a day about one fact that had not changed. An alerting
   channel that repeats itself is one an operator stops reading, and the fix was
   already written and simply not connected. readEscalationDeliveryState now
   reads the durable history and feeds it; the same ten ticks write four rows
   for four conditions.

2. There was no transport, only the literal `transport: 'UNCONFIGURED'`.

   Deciding to page someone and reaching them are different problems. The kernel
   solved the first and asserted the second as a string, so nothing could be
   configured, nothing attempted, and a delivery that failed was
   indistinguishable from one never tried.

   src/operator-escalation-transport.mjs is the transport half. It ships no
   transport that reaches a human device -- every such transport requires owner
   authorization this system does not hold, and a HUMAN_DEVICE transport without
   an authorization reference is refused outright rather than registered and
   skipped. What it does is make the gap addressable and loud: attempts produce
   durable receipts; "not configured", "tried and failed" and "tried and cannot
   tell" are three outcomes rather than one; a transport that throws is UNKNOWN,
   never FAILED, because a throw after the bytes left is not proof of
   non-delivery; and every transport is attempted even after one succeeds, since
   stopping at the first success discards the evidence that the others are
   broken.

   An escalation that reached nobody is now itself escalated, as CRITICAL
   OWNER_UNREACHABLE. A monitoring system that detects a critical condition and
   cannot tell anyone has two problems, and the second is worse. Its fingerprint
   deliberately excludes the undelivered count: feeding a growing list into the
   identity gave it a new fingerprint every cycle, which is a fresh escalation
   forever about being unable to send escalations.

3. Founder-absence readiness never asked whether the founder could be reached.

   A probe built a proof satisfying every dimension -- 900 successful ticks over
   31 days, zero unauthorized effects, zero dead letters, zero abandoned cycles,
   matching commit and policies, every capability VERIFIED_LIVE and externally
   verified -- and got KILIMANJARO_READY at 100%, nextGate
   RUN_OWNER_ABSENCE_CANARY, while nothing in the repository could reach a
   person. `ownerEscalationQueue` was satisfiable by the queue existing.

   undeliveredEscalations is now a required proof dimension, absent means
   refused rather than zero, and it is read from the durable page ledger rather
   than accepted as an assertion. ownerEscalationQueue joins EXTERNAL_PROOF_-
   REQUIRED: whether a page reached a person is the archetypal claim this system
   cannot make about itself.

Honest end state: the transport layer is real and tested; no human-reachable
transport is configured; the system now says so durably, escalates its own
inability to page, and refuses to call itself absence-ready while that holds.

commits.message:
Merge: four-state effect vocabulary and ledger consolidation

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01BvS8JECUaTUe25vYVxeBE9

commits.author: Claude
commits.message:
Distinguish zero, unknown, not-observed and occurred effects

A counter set to 0 answers "how many". It does not answer "did anyone look",
and the system was reading it as though it did. A worker that genuinely made
no provider calls and a worker that crashed between dispatch and receipt both
shipped providerCalls: 0, and both were accepted as proof that nothing reached
the outside world. The second is not proof of anything -- it is the exact shape
an already-delivered effect takes when nobody was watching.

src/effect-ledgers.mjs now classifies a complete ledger into one of four
states. A dimension declares non-observation by carrying a sentinel in place of
a number, so omitting a key stays a refusal: a sentinel is a declaration, not a
way to say nothing at all.

  ZERO_EFFECT          every dimension observed, every one zero. The only state
                       that may be treated as proof.
  EFFECT_OCCURRED      at least one positive count.
  EFFECT_UNKNOWN       may have happened, cannot be determined.
  EFFECT_NOT_OBSERVED  nobody looked.

isProvenZeroEffect is deliberately not `state !== EFFECT_OCCURRED`. Unknown and
not-observed are not weaker versions of zero; they are the absence of the
evidence that would make zero a claim at all.

Made load-bearing at the relay admission boundary. canonicalZeroEffectLedger
told all three refusals apart as nonzero-external-effect-ledger-rejected, which
accused an honest worker of making calls it never made and gave an operator no
way to see an uncertain execution at all. Three distinct reason codes now; the
historical vocabulary for occurred, malformed and incomplete ledgers is
unchanged, so existing callers and tests keep matching what they matched.

Also consolidated fifteen byte-identical local copies of ZERO_EXTERNAL_EFFECTS
onto the canonical module. Fifteen copies of a safety vocabulary is fifteen
places for it to drift, and it had already drifted once -- three spellings and
two known field names, which is how businessEffectLedger came to be rejected as
credential-bearing. A test now fails on the sixteenth copy.

Merge: remove autonomy persistence ceiling, close ratchet gate hole

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01BvS8JECUaTUe25vYVxeBE9

commits.author: Claude
commits.message:
Remove the autonomy persistence ceiling and close the ratchet's gate hole

Two P1 defects, both found by probing rather than by any failing test.

1. MAX_SCAN was a ceiling wearing a page size's name.

   Four modules each held a private MAX_SCAN and passed it straight through as
   store.list({ limit }). src/store.mjs _listDirect applies no ordering unless a
   caller passes orderBy, so rows arrive oldest-first and limit: 2000 returns the
   OLDEST 2000. Probed against the real modules:

   - 2100 filler snapshots then one new run: listLatestAutonomyRuns answered
     ok: true, status: 'LISTED' with the new run absent. Not a saturation error --
     a confident, complete-looking, wrong answer. A scheduler reading that listing
     could never see the run.
   - 2100 filler selections then three runs served: selectFairAutonomyRuns
     re-served 2 of those 3 immediately, because from inside the window they had
     never been served. That is the starvation bug the fairness ledger exists to
     prevent, returning at scale, silently.

   Raising the number moves the mark. src/durable-audit-scan.mjs removes it:
   callers fold rows into an accumulator as pages arrive, so the walk runs to
   exhaustion at memory bounded by distinct keys rather than history length, and
   a walk that cannot finish fails closed. listLatestAutonomyRuns now returns
   SCAN_SATURATED rather than a subset, and the scheduler returns
   FAIRNESS_LEDGER_UNREADABLE rather than guessing at an order it cannot justify.

   MAX_PAGES in the scanner is a liveness guard, not a data ceiling: exceeding it
   is a refusal with a reason code, never a truncated success.

   tests/autonomy-scheduler-starvation-bound.test.mjs had a fake store that
   ignored offset. offset is part of the store contract -- implemented on the JSON
   path and as SQL OFFSET on the Postgres path -- so the fake was fixed, not the
   guard. Its newest-first reversal is kept deliberately: the walk must not depend
   on an ordering no store promises.

2. The reachability ratchet accepted any invented gate name.

   AWAITING_ACTIVATION required only that `gate` be truthy. A probe set
   gate: "TODO_FIGURE_THIS_OUT_LATER" and all seven ratchet tests passed, which
   made AWAITING_ACTIVATION a resting state reachable by typing anything -- the
   exact failure the ratchet exists to prevent, a decision that was never made
   wearing the shape of one.

   Gates are now declared in config/reachability-classification.json with what
   they block and what would release them. Minting one is a reviewable edit to a
   registry rather than a string typed into one module. Four new tests enforce it.

   The two remaining NEEDS_TRIAGE entries are resolved on evidence that predates
   this pass: docs/AGENT_MESH_REACHABILITY_TRIAGE.md already recorded the ordering
   decision for agent-evolution-wave and the external-effect exclusion for
   ai-access-opportunity-registry. Reasons cite that record rather than restating
   confidence.

commits.author: Claude
commits.message:
Stop one provider event clearing as revenue twice

reconcilePaymentRenewalTruth requires three witnesses before it will call money
cleared: an order, a payment_classification receipt, and a revenue ledger row,
all keyed on eventName:eventId. The first two are keyed maps and therefore
deduped. The revenue ledger is a list, and it was not.

Two rows carrying the same providerEventId each matched the same order and the
same receipt, and both were counted. Probed: a single $50 payment recorded twice
reported $100 cleared, with contradictions empty. For a module whose entire
purpose is cleared-revenue truth, that is the defect that matters most.

Verified rows are deduped by provider event now, and a duplicate is not silently
dropped either - it is a ledger integrity problem in its own right, so it raises
duplicate-revenue-rows-for-one-provider-event and the count and cents are
reported. Twelve duplicates of one event still clear exactly once; two genuinely
different events still clear twice.

The module also declared its own effect-ledger shape with an extra
paymentMutations key. paymentMutations is a real effect it needs to report and
the canonical set does not carry, and adding it there would make every existing
complete ledger incomplete under the relay's own contract. So it spreads the
canonical shape and declares the one extension, rather than retyping a fourth
independent copy - if the canonical set changes this follows it. A test pins
that the extension is exactly one key wide.

Found by attacking code that had already merged green. The gate was right that
nothing was broken; it had no opinion about whether the arithmetic was true.

commits.author: Claude
commits.message:
Close three laundering paths a parallel session found

A second Kilimanjaro closure branch ran the same mission independently. Merging
it would mean a third implementation of nearly everything, so it is not merged.
Three of its findings describe defects that are real in this tree, and those are
fixed here.

The sandbox destroyer was a delete primitive wearing a cleanup label. It
required the target basename to start with uberbond-sandbox- and checked
nothing else, so any directory anywhere with that name was destroyable. Probed:
it deleted a directory the provisioner never created, containing a file it had
never seen. Membership in the set of workspaces this process actually created
is the authority to delete now. That set is in-process and lost on restart,
deliberately: a leaked temp directory is a far smaller problem than a recursive
delete pointed at the wrong path.

The causal graph accepted a hand-typed payment as an economic anchor. Truth
level, a positive integer amount, a three-letter currency and a provider event
id all pass on an object typed by hand, so the apparatus built to stop revenue
being invented was checking only whether the invention was well-formed. Probed:
a literal became a five-thousand-dollar anchor. A real outcomeId is a digest of
the commercial-outcome policy version and the provider event id, so it
recomputes; requiring that means a forger must produce the receipt the compiler
would have produced. Revenue is still forgeable by whoever controls the
provider event id. It is no longer forgeable from nothing.

sourceType and evidenceClass were two independent strings a caller set, so a
search-engine snippet could file itself as DIRECT_FIRST_PARTY, enter the direct
evidence set, and manufacture a conflict against a company's own team page. A
class is a claim about where something came from and the source already says
that. Declared classes are clamped to what the source supports, and the clamp
is recorded rather than silent. Declaring a weaker class is still allowed:
trusting something less is always permitted.

commits.author: Claude
commits.message:
Attenuate every authority dimension, not just constraints

The worker-scope branch had been open since 21 August and carried two things
worth having: pending relay results are scoped to the worker context that owns
them, and a child task's authority attenuates rather than merely inheriting.

It conflicted with the constraint work in four places because it predated it,
and the resolution is the union rather than either side. Constraints keep the
fail-closed union from inheritTaskConstraints, which refuses at the ceiling
instead of trimming a parent's restriction away. Forbidden actions and the
token budget are new dimensions and attenuate the same way: a child may request
less than its parent and can never request more.

The branch's own local constraint union is removed rather than kept alongside.
Two implementations of one rule with different bounds is how the quieter copy
ends up dropping a restriction, which is the defect this whole area exists to
prevent.

Verified end to end: a child asking for 500000 tokens against a 40000-token
parent gets 40000, and inherits all eleven forbidden actions and all three
constraints despite requesting none.
