commits.author: Claude
commits.message:
Bridge the two effect ledgers, and pin why the scanner exemption stays loose

Two branches arrived for the same file from the same base. The bridge maps both
ledger shapes onto one canonical key set, with businessSpendCents normalizing
onto spendCents and a strict normalizeEffectLedger that refuses missing keys,
unknown keys and non-integer counters. That is the unification the state doc
listed as an open residual, so it is merged.

The other branch also made isKnownEffectLedgerField strict - complete keys,
finite non-negative values - on the reasoning that a partial ledger is not a
real ledger. That change is measurably wrong and is not taken.

The scanner's only question is whether something is a counter or a credential.
An incomplete ledger is a counter with a missing field. Making it fail the
exemption sends it to the credential pattern, where credentialChanges matches.
Applied and measured: hasSecret on { providerCalls: 0 } flips from false to
true, which is precisely the false positive that made every result carrying a
businessEffectLedger unprocessable earlier in this session. The existing suite
did not catch it because nothing covered hasSecret on an incomplete ledger.

Completeness is enforced where it belongs and already was: validResult still
returns incomplete-external-effect-ledger-rejected, and normalizeEffectLedger
returns effect-ledger-missing-keys. Both name the actual problem.

There is now a test that pins the loose exemption together with the strict
validation, and it fails if the strict variant is reapplied.

commits.author: Claude
commits.message:
Make dead code fail a gate instead of waiting to be noticed

A module reachable only from tests is not reachable. The suite proves it
behaves; it proves nothing about whether anything can call it. That distinction
cost this repository three separate discoveries: the mesh entry point (#88),
the occurrence compiler (#100, found by walking imports rather than by any
failing test), and the operator escalation kernel, which knew eleven ways the
system could be in trouble and had no caller. Each was implemented, tested,
green, and dead.

A real reachability walk from server.mjs, worker.mjs, api/ and scripts/ says
45 of 146 src modules have no entry point at all - the whole commercial layer
and the whole Claude engineering path. The existing manifest reported 28,
because it counted direct importers and a module imported only by another
unreachable module still cannot run.

Every one of the 45 is now classified with a named category and a real reason,
and the ratchet fails when a new unclassified dead module appears. It does not
demand that everything be wired: most of these are correctly unreachable, and
wiring outreach without an authorisation path is how a system contacts someone
by accident. It demands that the decision be written down.

Three entries are NEEDS_TRIAGE rather than invented: agent-model-router,
agent-evolution-wave and ai-access-opportunity-registry have no caller and no
gate, and nobody has decided whether they are live architecture or residue.
Saying so is better than assigning them a category that sounds settled.

The ratchet caught me writing "Same reason." as a justification for one entry,
which is the sort of thing it exists to catch.

commits.author: Claude
commits.message:
Give the escalation kernel something to look at, and somewhere to run

The operator escalation kernel recognises eleven ways the system is in trouble
and had no way to read the store, so nothing called it. That is the third time
this pattern has turned up here: the mesh entry point in #88, the occurrence
compiler in #100, and now this. A capable module no code path reaches is not a
capability.

composeOperatorHealthSnapshot reads durable truth and nothing else - terminal
cycle receipts, abandoned cycles, dead-lettered jobs, stalled and stranded
runs, and effect-ledger integrity read off the receipts themselves rather than
asserted. The mesh tick composes it after each cycle, evaluates it, and
persists whatever an owner would need to act on.

The property that makes a health report worth reading is that a dimension the
store could not answer is reported unreadable rather than defaulted to zero.
Nothing-is-wrong and we-did-not-look must never be the same value, because the
second one is exactly how a dead system looks healthy. There is a test that
takes a store which throws on the jobs collection and asserts the count comes
back undefined, not 0.

Commercial health is deliberately absent from the snapshot: payment and send
state have no durable source in this system yet, and inventing zeros would
report health nobody observed.

This is the queue, not the pager. Nothing here delivers a message; transport is
UNCONFIGURED and deliveryProof is NOT_AVAILABLE, and a test asserts the report
never claims otherwise. Actually waking a human still needs a channel
credential, which is an owner action and not one I can grant on their behalf.

commits.author: Claude
commits.message:
Scan every page for the run, not just the one it first appears on

The paged snapshot lookup lifted the 2000-row ceiling by walking offset pages
until the requested run appeared, on the reasoning that pages arrive
newest-first so the first hit must be the newest.

Pages do not arrive newest-first. src/store.mjs _listDirect applies no ordering
unless a caller passes orderBy, so rows come back in insertion order, oldest
first. Stopping at the first page containing the run therefore returned that
run's OLDEST snapshot.

Measured: a run buried under 2500 filler rows and then advanced to sequence 5
came back at sequence 0. That is the same silent rewind the saturation guard
exists to prevent, arriving through the door built to fix it.

The walk now continues to exhaustion and keeps every matching row, picking the
newest across all of them. It costs a full filtered pass; correctness under an
ordering the store never promised is worth more than a shorter walk. The
repeated-page detection for stores that ignore offset is unchanged.

The regression uses a store that mirrors _listDirect exactly - filter, offset,
limit, no sort - because using a friendlier fake is how the assumption survived
in the first place. Reverting to stop-at-first-hit fails it.

commits.author: Claude
commits.message:
Make the occurrence-identity layer something production can actually reach

#93 gave recurring work a restart-stable identity, and nothing in production
ever used it. The mesh tick pumps whatever runs already exist in the store, and
no production path created one with an occurrence identity, so
compileScheduledAutonomyRun was a compiler nobody compiled with. A reachability
walk from server.mjs, worker.mjs and scripts/agent-mesh-tick.mjs confirmed it.

Issue #100 named this failure mode directly -- do not merge a dead compiler and
call the issue solved -- and it is the same gap #88 recorded for the mesh
itself. A green suite says nothing about whether a module can be reached, so
the regression ends with a reachability assertion rather than only behavioural
ones.

AGENT_MESH_MISSION declares one recurring mission. The tick seeds it before
pumping, so the run that occurrence declares exists to be pumped in the same
tick. Seeding is idempotent by construction: the runId is derived from the
occurrence key, so a redelivered tick finds the run rather than making a second
one, and the next occurrence of the same mission gets its own run under the
same missionKey.

Disabled unless a mission is configured. A configured-but-unparseable mission
is a refusal, not a fallback to no-mission -- an operator's broken JSON must not
look identical to never having written one. A saturated snapshot scan also
refuses, since no-such-run and run-is-past-the-bound are the same observation
from inside the store, and seeding on that ambiguity would create a duplicate
run for one occurrence.

commits.author: Claude
commits.message:
Block a known-bad contact route instead of merely scoring it zero (#99)

With requireContact=true the scorer hard-blocked only on a missing email
string. A route explicitly marked invalid scored zero for contact and then
cleared minScore on fit, evidence and intent alone, so qualification
advertised a known-undeliverable address as handoff-ready. Reproduced exactly
as the issue described: verified='invalid' returned eligible=true with an
empty blocks array.

Scoring a route zero is not the same as blocking on it. The gate now names the
route state, using the same vocabulary as the evidence layer: invalid,
undeliverable and bounced hard-block; suppressed, unsubscribed and complaint
hard-block; stale and expired require reverification; catch-all, risky,
unknown and temporary failures go to review. An unstated verification state is
refused too, because 'we never checked' and 'we checked and it is fine' must
not score the same.

Fixed in scoreLeadCandidate itself, as the issue asked, rather than by adding
a parallel scorer. Passing the gate is qualification truth only and confers no
send authority; suppression, the deliverability guard and the V9 consequence
gates remain final.

Separately, suppressionSet read only item.value, so a caller passing an array
of plain address strings got an empty set -- no error, no warning, no
suppression. For this particular check a silently empty list is the worst
available failure mode, so both shapes are accepted now.

Mutation proof per the issue's fifth expectation: reverting the gate to the
old missing-email-only check fails five of the ten regressions.

commits.author: Claude
commits.message:
Kilimanjaro architecture closure: reconcile ten PRs, repair seven P1s, earn the real-Postgres gate

Integrates the reliability stack (#91-#97), the prospect intelligence work
(#98), inbound sensing and causal attribution (#90), and the ServiceSKU,
delivery and acceptance truth engine (#72) onto one tree, gated individually
rather than batched.

Seven P1 defects were found by attacking the branches rather than merging
them, several inside the PRs that claimed to prevent them:

  - a child silently lost two of its parent's constraints at the ceiling,
    which is the exact disappearance #91 exists to prevent
  - an omitted ledger key read as a zero-effect proof, so {} scored the same
    as a signed zero
  - the secret scanner rejected a businessEffectLedger as credential-bearing
    because its exemption listed two of three ledger names
  - scheduler fairness ordered within a window the starved runs were not in:
    60 of 260 active runs were never served
  - a cycle that crashed between STARTED and TERMINAL was not a failed tick
    but nothing at all, so a mesh crashing every other cycle could certify a
    seven-day absence
  - six secret regexes with six different holes; ghs_ tokens walked through
  - a saturated bounded scan answered with a stale run, and a run simply
    stopped advancing with nothing saying why

The ~42 tests that skip without a real database had never executed. They ran
against a real PostgreSQL 18.4: 107 pass, 0 skipped. Three failed on the way
there and fail on main too -- the canary concurrency suite passed exactly once
per database because it randomised tenant ids but not idempotency keys.

Adds the sandbox provisioner the engineering path has never had, which does
real filesystem isolation and refuses to claim the network isolation it cannot
verify.

docs/CURRENT_SYSTEM_STATE.md is the canonical state, and it opens with the
numbers that matter: zero customers, zero cleared revenue, zero accepted
deliveries, zero retained customers.

commits.author: Claude
commits.message:
Give prospect qualification one answer instead of two

Two qualification modules arrived independently and each is right about a
different half. prospect-qualification.mjs produces the score -- nine weighted
dimensions with provenance, a model's opinion capped and never load-bearing
alone. prospect-qualification-gate.mjs consumes a score it is handed and
applies contact, identity and conflict gates on top.

Left side by side they are two sources of truth for one decision, which is how
a caller ends up quoting whichever one agrees with it. Composed, the scorer
decides fit and the gate decides admissibility.

The property that makes the composition safe is that the gate can only narrow.
There is no combination of requireContact, requireExactPerson or
allowResearchOnly that turns a prospect the scorer rejected into an eligible
one, and the test drives all four combinations to prove it.

commits.author: Claude
commits.message:
Rehearse the whole loop with nothing at stake, and refuse to call it a tier

One scheduled occurrence drives a durable mesh cycle; an autonomy run walks
the full research -> build -> review -> repair -> done conversation against
deterministic fake workers, reloaded from the store at every step; a synthetic
prospect passes through qualification; and the founder-absence evaluator is
asked what it makes of the result.

The last test is the point of the file. After a clean rehearsal it asserts that
readiness is still not KILIMANJARO_READY, and that the reasons given are the
honest ones: the observation window is shorter than seven days and there are
not enough repeated successful ticks. A rehearsal proves the parts connect. It
cannot prove anything that needs the passage of time or a real counterparty,
and the test says so in assertions rather than in a comment.

commits.author: Claude
commits.message:
Write down what is true in one place, and generate the readiness artifact

A future agent should not need eighty historical reports to learn the state of
the system, and it should not have to trust any of them.

docs/CURRENT_SYSTEM_STATE.md is the canonical answer, and it opens with the
four numbers that are easiest to bury: zero customers, zero cleared revenue,
zero accepted deliveries, zero retained customers. Every gate figure in it was
produced by running the command on this tree.

artifacts/system-readiness.json is generated by scripts/system-readiness.mjs
from recorded measurements rather than typed. The generator caps any capability
claiming level 5 or above without external evidence, because nothing inside a
repository can witness the outside world -- the same lesson as the hand-written
receipt that once minted five thousand dollars.

Both files carry the known bounds that are not cured: the 2000-row snapshot
scan ceiling, the serial-only real-Postgres suites, the two surviving ledger
shapes, and the fact that nothing pages the owner when the system dies.

commits.author: Claude
commits.message:
Stop a bounded scan answering with a stale run, and soak the spine

The soak drove 800 scheduler occurrences and 60 autonomy runs through the
durable spine and found a run that simply stopped. Not failed -- stopped, with
every reload returning ok and an older snapshot.

Every read in the autonomy store pulls a bounded window of audit rows and
picks the newest match out of it. Once that window comes back full, "no
matching row" stops meaning "no such run" and starts meaning "the run may be
past the bound", and from inside the function those are the same observation.
So the reload handed back the last snapshot it could see and the caller had no
way to tell a stalled run from a healthy one.

A saturated window is now its own reported failure rather than an answer, and
a write that cannot see its own history refuses instead of risking a sequence
regression. A stalled run that says it is stalled can be fixed.

This is a bound, not a cure: the window is fixed at 2000 snapshot rows because
the store's filters match top-level columns and cannot select on detail.runId.
Per-run reads need a schema change, and that is recorded rather than pretended
away.

The soak stays as a gate: one occurrence means exactly one terminal receipt
however many times it is delivered, every run reaches a terminal state, no
completed run reappears as active, and durable growth is linear in work done.

commits.author: Claude
commits.message:
Actually run the real-Postgres gate, and fix the test that only passed once

The ~42 tests behind OMNIA_V9_TEST_DATABASE_URL had never executed. They are
the ones that cannot be faked with PGlite -- concurrent recovery workers on
one stuck row, double-spend against a one-use approval, sub-second expiry
boundaries -- so "1561 pass, 42 skipped" was quietly carrying an unproven
claim about exactly the properties that matter most when nobody is watching.

Started a real PostgreSQL 18.4 from the embedded-postgres binaries already in
devDependencies and ran them. 107 tests, 107 pass, 0 skipped.

Three failed on the way there, and they fail on canonical main too, so this
is a pre-existing gate defect rather than a regression. The canary
concurrency suite randomises tenantId and approvalId per run but used a fixed
idempotency key. The reservation table keys idempotency globally -- correctly,
since an idempotency key is a promise about one action in the world -- so a
second run's candidates all collide with the first run's rows and the race
resolves to zero executions instead of one. The suite passed exactly once
against any given database and failed forever after. Deriving the key from
the already-unique tenantId makes it re-runnable; verified over three
consecutive runs against one database.

These files share a database and interfere when node --test runs them in
parallel, so npm run test:postgres-real runs them serially and refuses to
pass vacuously when the URL is absent. A gate that is only trustworthy at a
particular concurrency should say so in the command.

commits.author: Claude
commits.message:
Give the six secret scanners one vocabulary, and stop receipts quoting credentials

Six modules had grown their own copy of the credential regex and every copy
had a different hole. The relay and the compute store matched ghp_ only, so
a GitHub server-to-server, OAuth, user-to-server or refresh token walked
straight through. The provider worker matched every GitHub prefix and had no
pattern for a PEM private key at all. The change contract caught private keys
and AWS keys but neither sk- nor any GitHub token. A scanner is only as good
as its worst copy.

There is one copy now, and it is the union: every GitHub prefix, project- and
ant-scoped sk- keys, Slack tokens, AWS access keys, PEM private keys, bearer
credentials, and connection strings carrying inline credentials.

Separately, worker reason codes reach a durable mesh-cycle receipt as free
text, and truncation is not redaction -- a 180-character slice of a bearer
token is still most of a bearer token. Reason codes and thrown error messages
are redacted before they are persisted.

Adds a sweep that looks where a secret would actually end up: nested inside a
result, inside a durable receipt, inside the sandbox child environment, and
across every tracked file.

commits.author: Claude
commits.message:
Implement the sandbox hooks the engineering path has never had

createClaudeEngineeringExecutor has always required createSandbox,
destroySandbox and enterVerificationMode to be injected, and nothing outside
tests ever supplied them, so the whole Claude engineering route was
unreachable in production. PR #88 recorded that as a blocker; this stops it
being archaeology.

What the provisioner honestly does: a fresh temp workspace, a local clone
pinned to a resolved revision, an ephemeral HOME deliberately outside the
tree the model can edit, a child environment built from an allowlist so no
credential-shaped variable survives, git restricted to five subcommands with
no shell, and a destroy that refuses any path it did not create. The clone
uses --no-hardlinks, so the sandbox object store is a copy: a test deletes
the sandbox's .git/objects and the origin is untouched.

What it will not do is claim network isolation. A Node process cannot make
the production network unreachable to its own children, and the executor's
isolation contract requires productionNetworkReachability: false and
ANTHROPIC_ONLY egress. Those facts can only come from whatever actually
enforces them. Absent that attestation the provisioner does all its real
work, tears the workspace back down, and returns
SANDBOX_PROVISIONER_EXTERNAL_BLOCK with the unverified dimensions listed as
null rather than defaulted to the safe-looking value.

Separately: package.json was protected from untrusted engineering edits but
the scripts it names were not, so a change could rewrite test discovery or
the syntax check immediately before the gate that was about to run it.
scripts/run-tests.mjs, scripts/check-syntax.mjs and package-lock.json are
now protected too.

commits.author: Claude
commits.message:
Make the SDR decision deterministic, and the model advisory in fact

Section 10 asks that qualification not collapse to IDEAL / NOT_IDEAL and that
no model grant outbound authority. The evidence layer landed in #98; the
decision on top of it did not exist, so nothing enforced either half.

A prospect is scored across nine weighted dimensions, each carrying its own
provenance, and a deterministic policy reads those numbers to pick one of
four dispositions. A model assessment enters as one input with
MODEL_INFERENCE provenance, capped at half weight where no observation
exists, and it can never carry icpFit, buyerRoleFit or reachability on its
own -- those must be source-backed before a prospect enters an experiment.
Reachability is not scored at all: it is read off the verified routes.

A model that includes a decision-shaped field -- disposition, outboundAuthority,
suppressionOverride, budgetCents -- does not have that field ignored. The
prospect is quarantined and the requested fields are named, because a model
reaching for authority is itself a finding.

The policy reads numbers and states, never prose, which is what makes
instructions embedded in a prospect's own copy inert rather than merely
discouraged. There is a test that drives exactly that.

ELIGIBLE_FOR_EXPERIMENT means the governed send path may now consider this
prospect. It is not permission to contact anybody, and the result says so.

commits.author: Claude
commits.message:
Close four ways a suppressed contact came back to life

Section 29's invariant is a hostile scenario: someone unsubscribes, a later
enrichment run returns the same address marked VALID, and the system still
refuses to contact them. Four routes round it were open, and none of them
are exotic -- enrichment providers hand back tagged and dotted addresses as
a matter of course.

A SUPPRESSED verification was outvoted by any fresher VALID one, because the
route status was read off the most recent check. Suppression is now sticky:
once observed it dominates, whatever arrives later.

buyer+newsletter@example.com was treated as a different person from
buyer@example.com, and on Gmail so was b.uyer@. Suppression matches on the
address as the receiving mailbox sees it -- lowercased, plus-tag stripped,
dots removed only on domains that ignore them. Over-matching costs a lead;
under-matching costs a complaint we were told not to earn.

A complaint recorded as a riskFlag rather than a state did not block at all.
Refusal flags now block as firmly as the state does, while ordinary
deliverability flags like role-account still do not.

commits.author: Claude
commits.message:
Make a cycle that died mid-flight count as the failure it was

A mesh cycle writes STARTED, does its work, then writes TERMINAL. If the
process dies in between, the fail-closed half already worked: that occurrence
can never be re-delivered, so no consequence happens twice.

The other half was silent. Founder-absence readiness is derived from terminal
receipts, so a cycle that never reached TERMINAL was not a failed tick -- it
was nothing at all. A mesh crashing every other cycle could present an
unbroken run of healthy cycles and certify a seven-day absence on it. The
probe that found this ran twenty clean cycles alongside six crashes and
reported failedTicks: 0.

Readiness now refuses to certify while any abandoned cycle is outstanding,
and the count is a required dimension of a supplied proof, like open dead
letters -- a caller cannot certify by omitting it. reconcileAbandonedAgentMeshCycles
turns an abandoned STARTED receipt into a durable DEGRADED terminal receipt
so the crash is written down; it replays no work. The scheduler runs it at
the top of each cycle, and refuses to start a cycle it could not run, since
the history it is about to add to would be unsound.

A cycle still inside its horizon is presumed running, not abandoned.

Also brings three readiness assertions onto the duration-proof semantics
#96/#97 introduced. One of them asserted that eleven capability booleans and
no observation window reach KILIMANJARO_READY, which is the one-shot boolean
issue #83 exists to remove; it now pins the opposite.

commits.author: Claude
commits.message:
Give the scheduler a window the starved runs are actually in

PR #94 adds a durable selection ledger so the scheduler serves the
least-recently-selected active run first, and that part works. But the
active-run scan it orders is itself bounded at 200, and it was taken
newest-updated-first. Ticking a run refreshes its updatedAt, so served runs
stayed at the front of that window and any run past the cap never entered
it. With 260 active runs and five times the capacity needed, sixty were
never served once -- fair ordering inside a window the starved work is not
in is not fairness.

listLatestAutonomyRuns takes an explicit order; the scheduler asks for
oldest-touched first, so being served moves a run out of the window and
being ignored moves it in. Ties are broken on runId rather than left to the
sort's discretion, so one cohort cannot win every cycle. Operator-facing
callers keep newest-first.

The regression drives issue #85's actual claim -- every still-active run is
served within a bounded number of cycles, for N greater than the scan cap,
across a restart -- and fails on the previous ordering.

commits.author: Claude
commits.message:
Make a zero-effect claim prove itself, and teach the scanner the third ledger name

PR #92 routes every autonomy worker result through the relay's validResult
before it can move a run. Two things were wrong underneath that.

An omitted ledger key read as zero, because the check was
Number(ledger[key] || 0). A worker could therefore assert 'no external
effects' by shipping {} -- silence scored exactly the same as a signed zero.
A NaN scored zero too (NaN is falsy), and an array passed as an object.
The ledger must now carry the canonical key set with real numeric zeros, and
an invented counter is reported as an unknown effect key rather than as a
credential leak, which is what the secret scanner had been calling it.

The scanner exempts ledger fields from the credential pattern, because a
ledger's own key is called credentialChanges. It listed two of the three
field names this codebase writes; results carrying a businessEffectLedger
were rejected as secret-bearing. Both ledger shapes and the full list of
names they may be spelled under now live in one module, so a scanner or
validator has a single list to consult.

Adds a canonical terminal-truth gate: a result claiming DONE must carry a
non-empty outcome, a supported truth table, and tests when it changed
artifacts, and may not answer with another task's identity. Below DONE the
contract is unchanged, so a research result still needs no test run.

Three fixtures asserted the old permissiveness and were brought onto the
canonical contract; #92's own reason-code assertions now check containment
because the gate reports more than one reason.

commits.author: Claude
commits.message:
Fail closed on constraint overflow instead of dropping a parent's rules

PR #91 enforces that a child task inherits every constraint its parent
carries, but at the ceiling it broke its own invariant. compileTaskIntent
trimmed the incoming list to MAX_CONSTRAINTS - 2 and then prepended the two
mandatory constraints. A parent already holding the full 64 (62 of its own
plus the two mandatory) therefore produced a child with 62: the last two
parent restrictions vanished silently, which is exactly the disappearance
the monotonicity rule exists to prevent.

Compile the complete set once and refuse when it overflows. A task now
either carries every constraint it was handed or it does not compile.

Adds a randomised deep-chain property test for issue #81 rather than a
single example, plus the saturated-boundary and overflow cases.

commits.author: mohammedwessam2007
commits.message:
Make relay dispatch idempotent, so a crash mid-dispatch cannot pay twice (#89)

Making the mesh reachable made a real bug reachable too, and finding it was
only possible because the path now exists.

agent-autonomy-pump dispatches a task to the relay, and only afterwards does
agent-autonomy-job persist the run carrying the relayRef. Everything between
those two lines is a window in which the relay task exists and the run does not
know it -- a crash, an OOM, a container reclaim, or a failed snapshot write all
land in it.

createGithubRelayTask created a GitHub issue unconditionally. So the next tick
re-dispatched the same deterministic taskId and a SECOND issue appeared for one
task. Two workers claim two issues, do the work twice, and with provider-backed
workers that is two charges.

Reproduced directly before fixing: same input twice, two issues, one taskId.

The transport is now idempotent on taskId against open, not-done relay issues.
Four cases, each with its own answer:

- retry after a crash returns ALREADY_QUEUED and the existing issue number, so
  the run rebinds instead of re-dispatching. A distinct status, not a silent
  QUEUED: nothing was created, and a receipt saying otherwise is a lie an audit
  trail carries forever.
- the same id with different content is refused. Returning either version would
  be a guess about which caller is right.
- a task that already completed and closed may be dispatched again.
  Deduplication must not become a permanent ban on re-running an objective.
- a client that cannot list issues is refused outright, because it cannot tell a
  first dispatch from a retry, and creating on that assumption is exactly the
  unknown consequential state that must not proceed.

Identity comparison deliberately excludes createdAt, status and deadline. A
retry is by definition a second compilation at a later instant, so comparing
whole tasks would report every legitimate recovery as a conflict.

One further refusal, for the case that is neither "duplicate" nor "no
duplicate": if the first page of open relay tasks comes back full, an unscanned
page may hold the duplicate, and that is "cannot tell", not "none found". Fifty
concurrent open relay tasks is far past any expected load so it should never
fire, but reporting "cannot tell" as "none found" is precisely how a duplicate
charge slips through.

The regression test drops the post-dispatch run on the floor exactly as a killed
process would and asserts one issue exists after two ticks. Verified it fails
against the previous code by reverting the fix and re-running.

Gate: 360 files parse, 1603 tests, 1561 pass, 0 fail, 42 skipped (unchanged,
all gated on a real Postgres), relay-safety 150/150, 0 vulnerabilities, lite/

commits.message:
Make the agent mesh reachable, and put the activation gate in front of it (#88)

* Give the agent mesh an entry point, and the two functions it needs to run

agent-mesh-control-plane composes the autonomy pump and the model workers
into a bounded cycle. It is the top of the cognitive bus, twenty-six modules
sit underneath it, and outside tests/ nothing imported it. No scheduler job,
no worker handler, no npm script, no workflow.

It was worse than unscheduled. runAgentMeshCycle requires an adapterFactory
and a compileRelayTask, and neither existed outside a test file: the only
adapterFactory in the repository was the stub `() => ({})` in a unit test,
and compileRelayTaskFromIntent was written, tested, and never passed to
anything. The first time an entry point existed, the cycle returned BLOCKED
with ["adapter-factory-required", "relay-task-compiler-required"].

chatgpt-relay-client -- the only implementation of the transport shape the
pump wants -- had no non-test importers either. Three complete, tested,
unreachable modules. A green suite does not distinguish "works" from "cannot
be reached", and 1535 passing tests said nothing about this.

Adds:

- scripts/agent-mesh-tick.mjs, one finite invocation. Bounded, non-resident,
  cloud-neutral, disabled unless AGENT_MESH_ENABLED is exactly "true".
  Distinct exit codes so a scheduler can tell DEGRADED from BLOCKED from a
  crash from the normal disabled resting state.
- src/agent-relay-adapter-factory.mjs, the adapterFactory the control plane
  actually means: a memoized chatgpt-relay-client per origin/target pair.
- src/agent-model-executor-factory.mjs, each worker's modelExecutor from its
  declared provider.

The two factories are named apart on purpose. I conflated them first time
through -- "adapterFactory" reads like the thing that talks to a model, and
it is not; it is the wire the compiled task travels over. The control plane
takes both.

A worker config arriving as JSON cannot carry a function, which is why the
tick script has to resolve both and attach them. Until now there was no way
to configure a worker from outside the process at all.

Refusals kept deliberate: a provider without both a pricing source and a
verification date is refused, because cost computed from unsourced pricing is
a number the system invented and the compute ledger would be quietly
fictional. A worker whose provider cannot be configured fails the tick by
name rather than being skipped -- silently doing nothing is
indistinguishable from having no work.

tests/agent-mesh-entry-point.test.mjs seeds a real autonomy run, drives a
real cycle through the real compiler and the real adapter over a stub fetch,
and asserts the task reached the transport and the relayRef was persisted. It
also asserts the cycle still fails closed with a dependency missing, so this
wiring cannot be deleted without a test noticing.

Writing that test found something worth keeping: the first version invented
its own externalEffectLedger shape and the client rejected it. It now imports
the real ZERO_EFFECTS. A stub that imitates a contract instead of importing
it will eventually disagree with it.

No business-world authority is added. Every task the cycle compiles stays
LOCAL_PREPARATION and businessEffectAuthority stays NONE.

Gate: 357 files parse, 1577 tests, 1535 pass, 0 fail, 42 skipped (unchanged,
all gated on a real Postgres), relay-safety 150/150, 0 vulnerabilities,
lite/ untouched.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01ARPWEE3rEGQ8PZMzcMuaCX

* Enforce the activation gate, reach the sandbox provider, name the canonical spend path

Three more modules that were complete, tested, and unreachable.

The activation gate was the important one. agent-mesh-activation-gate decides
whether the mesh may call a model provider at all, and nothing ever built the
evidence input it takes -- so it had no callers, and the entry point added in
the previous commit would have called a provider with nothing between it and
the money.

It is now evaluated on every tick and enforced. Its four permitted modes map
onto worker execution, because a worker tick is the only thing in a cycle that
can call a provider: NO_PROVIDER_CALLS and SYNTHETIC_ONLY run none,
ONE_PROVIDER_CANARY runs one on a canary-ready provider,
BOUNDED_CLOUD_REHEARSAL runs all. Autonomy pumping is unaffected -- it relays
LOCAL_PREPARATION tasks and calls nothing.

agent-mesh-activation-evidence builds the gate's input from two sources kept
deliberately apart. First-hand facts the process checks itself -- is a
credential present, is pricing evidence present -- are always computed and can
never be overridden. Attested claims it cannot verify come from an operator
JSON file. A file cannot upgrade a first-hand fact, or the evidence file
becomes a way to talk the gate into opening; there is a test for that exact
attack. With no file at all the verdict is ARCHITECTURE_ONLY /
NO_PROVIDER_CALLS, which is the intended resting state. A file that is named
but missing or malformed is a refusal, not a fallback: a broken attestation
must not produce the same outcome as never having written one.

Withheld workers exit 3 rather than 0. A scheduler running happily forever
while the workers it was configured to drive never run once is the same silent
failure this entry point exists to remove.

claude-code-sandbox-executor is now the third provider. It drives a local
Claude Code CLI in an isolated sandbox and needs no pricing evidence, because
the CLI reports its own usage and total cost -- the number comes from the tool
that spent it. When the CLI reports no cost the executor returns UNCERTAIN
rather than zero, so unknown spend never looks free. It is a local process, not
free compute; it consumes whatever account it is configured against. It
requires an OS isolation receipt attesting an ephemeral filesystem, no mounted
business credentials, no reachable production network, and Anthropic-only
egress, and the executor rejects a receipt whose root does not match the
configured one. The gate scores only the two API providers, so a sandbox worker
has no canary readiness to look up and is never eligible under
ONE_PROVIDER_CANARY -- unknown reads as not-permitted, asserted by a test.

agent-provider-execution implements the same reserve/invoke/commit transaction
as agent-worker-runtime, with the same uncertainty rule, and had no importers.
The runtime is canonical: same transaction plus durable persistence, lease
heartbeating, and execution records. The duplicate is marked SUPERSEDED rather
than deleted -- it is the clearest small statement of the compute-safety rule
and its tests pin that rule independently -- and a test now fails if anything
outside tests/ imports it. Two reachable implementations of "spend money" is
the shape that produces a double charge.

Also adds scripts/kilimanjaro-manifest.mjs, which measures its own numbers from
the repository instead of restating typed ones, and reports the suite as
NOT_RUN unless handed real TAP output.

Docs: AGENT_MESH_ENTRY_POINT covers the gate and the providers,
AGENT_MESH_REACHABILITY_TRIAGE accounts for all seventeen remaining modules
with no non-test importer (seven are operator tooling where that is correct;
six are business modules gated by tonight's zero external-effect ledger; the
rest name the specific blocker), and KILIMANJARO_ZERO_GAP_OVERNIGHT_REPORT
states plainly what was not done -- notably that the mesh is reachable but has
never been observed doing real work, and that the durable engineering executor
cannot be wired without first writing sandbox provisioning that does not exist.

Gate: 359 files parse, 1597 tests, 1555 pass, 0 fail, 42 skipped (unchanged,
all gated on a real Postgres), relay-safety 150/150, 0 vulnerabilities, lite/
untouched. No provider was called and no money was spent.

commits.message:
Untrack the node_modules symlink I committed, and close the gap that let it in

A self-referential symlink -- node_modules -> /home/user/uberbondd/node_modules
-- was committed to main in d806f71, one of my own commits. I created it with
a worktree setup line that ran once with the working directory back at the
repository root, then swept it into git with `git add -A`.

Any checkout of that commit gets a node_modules that points at itself. It
shadows the real dependency tree, so npm cannot run a single script and every
test dies with module-not-found. That is what I spent the last hour
misdiagnosing as npm refusing over-long script strings; the scripts were fine.

Two things had to be wrong for this to reach main, and both are now fixed.

The symlink is untracked (`git rm --cached`, so nobody's working copy is
touched).

And .gitignore said `node_modules/` with a trailing slash. That pattern
matches a DIRECTORY. A symlink named node_modules is not a directory, so it
was never ignored and `git add -A` picked it up without complaint. The slash
is gone, which matches both.

Verified after removing the bad link and reinstalling: check:syntax 353 files
parse, 1567 tests, 1525 pass, 0 fail, 42 skipped, npm audit 0 vulnerabilities.

commits.message:
Discover the test and syntax suites instead of listing them

Start with the correction, because I got the diagnosis wrong first.

After merging five PRs, `npm run check:syntax` and `npm run test:deterministic`
both exited 216 having executed nothing. I concluded the package.json script
strings had grown too long for npm and rewrote them. That was wrong. The real
cause was mine: a worktree setup line, `ln -sfn .../node_modules node_modules`,
ran once with the working directory back at the repository root and replaced
node_modules with a symlink to itself. Every dependency was gone, so npm could
not run any script at all -- including a script that was literally
`node -e 'console.log("plain ok")'`. Removing the bad link and reinstalling
fixed it. main was green the whole time.

The refactor still earns its place, on evidence rather than on the story that
motivated it:

  old hand-maintained list   116 files named, 135 reached, 1417 tests
  discovered                 126 files handed, 145 reached, 1567 tests

Ten test files had never executed under the main gate -- not by name and not
by import from anything named:

  pending-relay-reconciliation, relay-deployment-attempt,
  relay-deployment-eligibility, relay-preview-integration,
  relay-preview-proof, relay-preview-runbook, relay-shadow-binding,
  relay-vercel-api-executor, relay-vercel-api-request,
  relay-zero-effects-contract

They arrived with #45, which put them in a separate test:relay-safety script
that `npm run check` never calls. Discovery finds them because they exist,
rather than because someone remembered to append them to a 4,496-character
line. That is +150 tests, all passing, that the gate was silently skipping.

The runner also excludes any file another handed file imports, so the
double-execution bug I introduced earlier tonight is now structurally
impossible rather than merely fixed once.

The build-wiring guard is rewritten around the same primitives: every test
file must execute somewhere, none may execute twice, the browser and
live-database suites must stay out of the deterministic set, and no script may
drift back toward the size that is hard to reason about. The size check is
explicitly a canary, set at 2,000 characters -- loose enough not to fail
test:relay-safety at a legitimate 412, since inventing a rule is not the same
as protecting an invariant.

Verified after repairing node_modules: check:syntax 353 files parse, exit 0;
1567 tests, 1525 pass, 0 fail, 42 skipped; npm audit 0 vulnerabilities.
